utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Happy new year to everybody. We are going to begin the Aleksovski trial and ask now that the Registrar tell us the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now begin, and begin by the opening statement, if the Prosecutor wishes to make one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, this Prosecution concerns a violation of the laws and customs of war and the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, perpetrated by the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski. The crimes are alleged to have been committed in the Kaonik prison in the Lasva Valley area of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina between January and May 1993. During this time, the forces of the former allies, the Bosnian Croats, the HVO, backed by forces of the Republic of Croatia, the HV, engaged in open conflict with forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BiH. Zlatko Aleksovski was the commander of the Kaonik prison, which was used to detain persons, mostly of Muslim ethnicity, from villages such as Jelinak, Loncari, Strane, Skradno in the Lasva Valley area, which were displaced as a result of the conflict. In order to assist your Honours to better understand the case, I will illustrate on the television monitors some material that will be tendered as evidence in these proceedings, which will indicate some of the more important geographical locations relevant to this case. We have a series of those maps which can be shown on the screen, and if it pleases your Honours, I might go to those maps now, so that when I speak of these places, your Honours will have a better understanding as to the places where I refer. If your Honours could look at your screen now on the video monitor, the first map that I would ask to be displayed is map numbered A1/1. Your Honours, this is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is divided into the relevant opstinas. The opstina is a word meaning "municipality", and Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided into various municipalities. In the centre of these municipalities -- in the centre of this map are the three main municipalities which relate to the events of this case, and they are the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca and Zenica. If we can look at a blown-up version of those three opstinas, we can see them now, your Honours, more clearly. In the very centre of the map, your Honours can see the opstina of Vitez, Busovaca, Zenica and to some extent you may hear spoken of the surrounding opstinas of Travnik, Novi Travnik in the course of the evidence. Your Honours, in addition to opstinas named, there is also a reference in these maps to the main cities of the opstinas and those cities bear the same name as the opstinas themselves, so in Zenica you have the city of Zenica, which is one of the largest cities in the region; you have Vitez in the opstina of Vitez, and Busovaca in that relevant opstina as well. Your Honours, the Lasva Valley runs through -- primarily through the three opstinas of Vitez, Busovaca and it joins the Bosna River which then proceeds to run up through Zenica. If we could look at the next map, your Honours, that appears on the screen, A1/4, this, your Honours, is a map of the region, and if we can zoom in please on firstly the cities in the centre of the map of Strane, your Honours can see villages can be - if we have a better view of that, if we could mark the villages of Strane, it is towards the centre of the map. Your Honours can see that village. Then to the top of the map, the village of Loncari, right at the very top, the village of Jelinak, which is below that, Skradno, which is directly below Strane, and the little place of Kaonik, which is next to Strane. These are villages where people were captured and then subsequently imprisoned in the Kaonik prison. Through the centre of the map that now appears on your Honours' screen runs the Lasva River and it is hence the Lasva Valley. It runs down to a little place called Luke, which is now being shown on the screen, and that, your Honours, is where that river, the Lasva River, joins the Bosna River. This case, your Honours, is about the unlawful treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees. While detained at Kaonik, prisoners under the command of the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, many of the Muslim civilians and captured Muslim combatants, were subjected by prison guards and the HVO to treatment which amounted to an outrage upon their human dignity. The treatment was inhumane and included being kept in cramped and overcrowded facilities, being provided with inadequate food or water, being provided with inadequate or no medical treatment for the infirm or wounded, being subjected to physical or psychological abuse and intimidation; repeatedly being forced to dig trenches for the military forces, the HVO, at numerous and diverse locations, at or near lines of confrontation between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, thereby subjecting such detainees to death, injury, mental and physical harm; being subjected to use as human shields at diverse locations in the Lasva Valley area in order to protect HVO military installations or troops from forces hostile to the HVO and some being shot or beaten to death by the HVO. The Kaonik prison was a former JNA barracks, captured in the early part of the war. Your Honours, a photograph now appearing on the monitor is an aerial photograph taken of the Kaonik prison, and it is numbered A1/5. Your Honours, we will come back to this photograph in the course of the evidence, but it is in the centre of the screen that now appears. Your Honours, the Prosecution will show that members of the civilian population of the villages were imprisoned unlawfully and that many of these persons, once detained, along with those who were prisoners of war, were beaten and abused in Kaonik detention centre. The unlawful imprisonment of civilians, the beatings and torture and inhumane treatment, the forcible use of civilians for digging trenches and as human shields, the mental and physical abuse and anguish inflicted on the detained persons who were at all times protected by international humanitarian law, are the central focus of this indictment. The underlying conflict of the parties of the former Yugoslavia, the origin of the tragic hostilities among these nationalities of that unfortunate country and more specifically the HVO attacks on the Muslim population in the Lasva Valley area between January and May 1993, and the general harassment of Muslim population prior to Muslim civilians being rounded up and forcibly transferred to detention centres such as Kaonik are the background to the trial. To illustrate the Lasva Valley area that led to the incarceration in Kaonik prison of members of the Muslim population in the surrounding villages and to facilitate an understanding of why it happened, the Prosecution will bring during the course of the proceedings an expert witness. At this juncture, your Honours, I would like to briefly review the background before concentrating on Kaonik prison and the accused Zlatko Aleksovski's specific culpability in relation to Muslim detainees at the prison. The former Yugoslavia, comprising of six republics and two autonomous regions, due to nationalistic tensions, disintegrated rapidly to culminate in the tumultuous social and political events of the late 1980s and 1990s. Four of the republics, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Macedonia declared their independence, which was resisted vehemently by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, giving rise to bloody wars in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in particular. In Bosnia, the parties to the conflict were generally but not exclusively divided along ethnic lines. The Bosnian Serbs under the leadership of Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic sought to cleave out an independent entity known as the Republika Srpska. The Bosnian Serbs were supported in this endeavour by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its army, the People's Army of Yugoslavia, the JNA. Although the JNA was allegedly withdrawn under mounting pressure from Bosnia on 19th May 1992, this withdrawal was more show than substance, because Belgrade continued to support the VRS, the army of the Republic of Srpska with arms, munitions and supplies. It was the possession of these superior arms that the war machine of the JNA inherited by the VRS that gave the Bosnian Serbs a decided advantage at the outset of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Bosnian Serbs were opposed initially in unison by the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, who were under the direction of the central government located in Sarajevo. Because the Bosnian government was taken by surprise and because the Bosnian Serbs had superior armaments, the Bosnian Serbs made impressive territorial gains in Bosnia and took control over large swathes of territory. The Bosnian Croats, dissatisfied with the Bosnian government's weak response to the Serbian aggression, responded in 1991 by creating the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a quasi state with its military component the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, ostensibly for the defence of Croat interests. Your Honours, our evidence will show that the Bosnian Croats were provided with significant logistical and manpower support, political direction and diplomatic backing in their efforts. While the Bosnian Croats initially allied themselves with the forces of the central government to resist the Serbian onslaught, this alliance was short-lived and soon war ensued between the allies. The Lasva Valley Region is located in Central Bosnia, approximately 50 kilometres north west of Sarajevo and stretches over the municipalities of Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca. In addition the area in question includes Novi Travnik. Before the events that occurred in the period from January to April 1993, the HVO had joint military control with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina over the Lasva Valley. However, in April 1993 virtually all Bosnia-Herzegovina forces in the region were moved to the Bosnian Serb front-lines. The western front-line was 8 kilometres north west of Travnik, and the eastern front-line was immediately north east of Kiseljak. The HVO forces had a large extent of freedom of movement behind the lines. As a result of the co-ordinated attacks on 16th April 1993, the HVO acquired military control over the Lasva Valley. Units of the HVO were deployed in a series of attacks on the Muslim civilian population in the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, from January through May of 1993. The attacks were planned, widespread and systematic. The HVO units involved in the attacks were structured by the principle of unity of command and obligation to carry out decisions, commands and orders of superior commanders. Beginning in May 1992, HVO forces gradually and systematically took control of the political, economic and military power of the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca, by means of threats, intimidation and assaults on Muslim persons and their property. They established HVO municipal leadership in Busovaca in May 1992, in Vitez in the fall of 1992, and in Novi Travnik in October 1992. In January 1993, HVO soldiers systematically rounded up the remaining Muslim population in the town of Busovaca and the surrounding villages of Kacuni, Merdani and Strane, which towns were mentioned earlier and shown on those maps, your Honours. Muslim businesses were destroyed and Muslim men were killed. Hundreds of Muslim civilians were detained in the Kaonik prison. Some were interrogated, some were beaten, some were taken to dig trenches and others were used as human shields. The Muslim civilians left in the area were continuously harassed from January through May 1993. Many Muslims were forced out of their homes and were arrested, and others were killed. The accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, was an official of the Zenica prison from 23rd February 1987, until leaving to be commander, director of the Kaonik prison near Busovaca towards the end of January 1993. At the same time the HVO arrested and confined hundreds of Muslim civilians from Busovaca in the Kaonik prison. Some of the detainees taken to dig trenches were mistreated at that time. It is the Prosecution case that Zlatko Aleksovski knew that detainees were being used as human shields. Being in charge of the prison, he was in a position of superiority to everyone else in the prison. As prison commander, he met with international officials and provided them with lists of detained persons and acknowledged his position as commander, director of the facility and of his understanding of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the detention and treatment of detainees in his charge. He freely admitted his knowledge that civilians were being sent to dig trenches when questioned by international officials. On January 1993, HVO soldiers arrested civilian males in the village of Ocenici. Eventually these and other arrested civilians were taken to Kaonik prison for detention. Although one prisoner received medical attention for injuries inflicted during his arrest, other prisoners could be heard screaming as a result of being beaten. Beatings and mistreatment also took place while Zlatko Aleksovski was still in command of Kaonik after selected civilian detainees arrived at Kaonik from Vitez municipality in May 1993. These detainees had been moved from the detention facility in Vitez. The attacks against the Muslim civilian population in Busovaca continued throughout the period from January 1993 to May 1993. Male civilians were rounded up and taken to Kaonik for detention, where they were subjected to inhumane conditions and mental and physical abuse. Turning now, your Honours, to the charges, the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, a native Bosnian Croat, and commander of the Kaonik prison, was required to abide by the mandate of the laws and customs governing the conduct of wars, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. However, Aleksovski, between January and May 1993, individually and in concert with others, planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of the unlawful treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees in the Lasva Valley area of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, Zlatko Aleksovski's responsibility for the crimes against identified persons could arise not only from his direct participation in such crimes, dealt with by Article 7(1) of the Statute, but also by virtue of his position of authority, where the evidence suggests not a direct involvement but a failure to prevent such crimes. The latter principle of individual responsibility for omission long recognised under international criminal law is reaffirmed by Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. By these acts and omissions, Zlatko Aleksovski committed grave breaches under Count 8 of the Geneva Conventions as recognised by Article 2(B), inhumane treatment, under 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The elements of inhumane treatment are that the offender, with intent, committed a specified act or omission that caused the physical, intellectual or moral integrity of the victim to be impaired, or caused the victim to suffer indignity, pain or suffering out of proportion to the treatment expected of one human being to another. Count 9, grave breach as recognised by Article 2(C), wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health, under liabilities under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The elements of wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health are that the offender with intent committed a specified act or omission upon a protected person which resulted in the victim being seriously injured or being subjected to great suffering. Count 10, a violation of the laws or customs of war, outrages on the personal dignity, as recognised by Article 3 of the Statute and under Article 7(1), 7(3) of the Statute. The elements of unlawfully inflicting outrages upon the personal dignity of the victim are that the offender committed an act or omission with the intention of unlawfully subjecting the victim to humiliating or degrading treatment. The theory of liability under Article 7(1) and 7(3) will be discussed momentarily. Your Honours, the Appeal Chamber in the Tadic has decided that Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal only applies to offences committed within the context of international conflict. We will provide evidence that shows that an international armed conflict between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia existed during the period of time when the offences referred to in the indictment are alleged to have been committed. Then furthermore, our evidence will demonstrate that the victims of the alleged offences were, for the purposes of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, protected persons linked to the Bosnian side of the conflict, while the alleged perpetrators had a nexus with the Bosnian Croat authorities and the Bosnian Croat entity was in fact linked to Croatia. The alleged offences are grave breaches because they are acts prohibited by the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Conventions committed against protected persons on the Bosnian side of the international conflict by persons with a link or nexus to the Croatian side. I may now pass for a moment to the personal details of the accused. The accused Zlatko Aleksovski was born on 8th January 1960 in Pakrac municipality in the Republic of Croatia. After Zlatko Aleksovski was born his parents moved from Pakrac to Zenica, where they were employed at the Zenica Zelezara ironworks. Zlatko Aleksovski completed elementary school and secondary school for electrical engineering in Zenica and then enrolled in the Veljko Viahovic Faculty of Political Sciences, Department of Sociology, in Sarajevo. He completed his studies on 28th September 1983 and qualified as a sociology teacher. Zlatko Aleksovski was first employed on 29th July 1985 at the Vatrostalna firm in Busovaca where he worked as Secretary for Information until 16th May 1986. From 23rd February 1987, he was employed as counsellor at the Zenica correction house until on or about January 1993, when he left to become commander of the prison facility at Kaonik near Busovaca. Your Honours, the accused, Aleksovski, has been charged under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. Dealing firstly with individual criminal responsibility, under Article 7(1) of the Statute, a person who plans, instigates, orders or commits, or otherwise aids or abets in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime described in the Statute is individually criminally responsible. Article 7(1) encompasses the principle that all those who contribute to the commission of the crime should be held individually responsible. The words "planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted" should be interpreted as all persons who take part in the commission of a crime are amenable to the criminal law. Courts generally do not strictly define the precise parameters of individual criminal responsibility, as the most marginal act of assistance or encouragement could amount to complicity. Mere presence at the scene of the crime without proof of other factors does not give rise to criminal liability; however presence at the scene of the crime, depending on the circumstances, may constitute criminal responsibility. There is a clear distinction between a bystander who happens to arrive at the scene of the crime and an individual who is intentionally present at a location where unlawful acts are being committed. Our evidence against the accused for Article 7(1), responsibility for the crimes in the indictment, is based on both direct testimonial and strong circumstantial evidence. First, Zlatko Aleksovski was the commander of the Kaonik prison. Our evidence will show that Aleksovski introduced himself to detainees and to international observers as the commander of the camp. Our evidence will also show that the prison guards were subject to Zlatko Aleksovski's orders. Nothing apparently could be carried out without his consent. The accused kept a tight control over events in the camp, he was experienced and trained as a prison warden. He knew how to run such an establishment. Guards were not permitted to embark on new initiatives without first obtaining Aleksovski's permission. The evidence will show that the HVO came into the cells at the Kaonik prison and took certain people out and beat them. It is the Prosecution case that these beatings occurred with the knowledge and/or acquiescence of the accused. It is the Prosecution's contention that the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed with impunity in a systematic manner. The crimes included the systematic detention of Muslim men and boys, both military and civilian; the widespread beating and mental and physical abuse of Muslim detainees by prison guards at Kaonik and HVO soldiers; the systematic use of Muslim detainees to dig trenches and to act as human shields. Your Honours, the inhumane treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees at Kaonik, which prevailed prior to Aleksovski's command over Kaonik prison, continued during the period January to May 1993 while he was commander. Passing now on to superior or command responsibility, your Honours, we have also alleged command responsibility. Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal elaborates the general provisions of Article 7(1) by specifically providing that superiors may be held criminally liable for the violations of international humanitarian law committed by their subordinates. It is a species of liability applicable under international criminal law in that it provides that a superior's failure to adequately control or punish subordinates may amount to an acquiescence in the offence committed by such subordinates, and a superior may accordingly assume criminal responsibility for these offences. Zlatko Aleksovski's position of authority in the Kaonik prison makes him responsible through his subordinates for acts and omissions where imprisonment, physical and mental abuse, use of detainees for trench digging and so on related to the very conditions of detention are concerned. All military commanders have a solemn obligation to ensure that the horror of war is not visited upon innocent civilians and prisoners of war -- and that they may be held responsible for a dereliction of duty, as was stated in the Yamashita case, and I quote: "It is evident that the conduct of military operations by troops whose excesses are unrestrained by the orders or efforts of their commander would almost certainly result in violations which the purpose of the law of war is to prevent. Its purpose to protect the civilian population and prisoners of war from brutality would largely be defeated if the commander of an invading army could with impunity neglect to take reasonable measures for their protection." The principle of command responsibility is enshrined in Article 7(3) and holds that a superior is criminally responsible if he knew or had reason to know that a subordinate was about to commit crimes or had done so and failed to take the reasonable or necessary steps to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. Although the term "command responsibility" is often a military term, it is used with respect to the present case and the position of the Prosecutor is that this doctrine also applies mutatis mutandis to civilians in positions of superior authority. In other words, command responsibility is the military expression of the broader concept of superior responsibility. The reference to superiors is sufficiently broad to cover military commanders or other civilian authorities who are in a similar position of command and exercise a similar degree of control with respect to their subordinates. To establish this form of criminal liability under the Statute, we have to and will establish the following three matters: the superior/subordinate relationship; first, the superior concerned must be the superior of the subordinate. Article 7(3) applies to superiors who have a personal responsibility in relation to perpetrators on the basis that the perpetrators are subordinate under the superior's control. The doctrine of superior responsibility is applicable with regard to subordinates under the direct or indirect control of the superior. Both forms of control can exist as a result of de jure or de facto chains of command. Your Honours, our evidence will show beyond a reasonable doubt that Zlatko Aleksovski was the commander of the Kaonik prison between the end of January and 31st May 1993. As such, Aleksovski was the highest officer in command of the prison. Zlatko Aleksovski, as demonstrated, exercised his control over the detention facility, Kaonik prison, in a variety of ways, including but not limited to formal meetings with international agencies, accepting the custody of arrested persons, allowing the unlawful interrogation of detained persons, allowing them to be used for unlawful forced labour, digging trenches, and to be used as human shields. He can be held criminally responsible under Article 7(3), irrespective of whether his position as camp commander can be characterised as superior, civilian superior, military commander or warden. The evidence will show that he had control over the guards and the persons in the camp who were his subordinates and he was under a duty to prevent or punish their violations of international humanitarian law. Your Honours may note that in the Hostages Case, the military tribunal there clearly held that an occupational commander endowed with executive power over occupied territory is responsible for acts committed within his area of responsibility, regardless of whether the unit was subordinated to his command or not. Further, Article 87 of Protocol 1 of 1977 extends the duty of commanders not only to members of the armed forces under their command but also to other persons under their control, implying that such commander is responsible for restoring and ensuring public order and safety as far as possible and shall take all measures in his powers to achieve this, even with regard to troops which are not directly subordinate to him, if these are operating in his sector. In addition to members of the armed forces, such responsibility would equally apply to local population, where for example some of the inhabitants were to undertake some sort of pogrom against minority groups. We say, your Honours, that by analogy the position that would operate in a camp with people entering the camp and carrying out acts in that camp, which camp is under the direct control of the accused, is an analogous circumstance. It is interesting, your Honours, that not only does Article 87 of Protocol 1 of the 1977 Protocol deal with this issue, but it also reflects the provisions of our own Statute, when in paragraph 3 it says that the high contracting parties and the parties to the conflict shall require any commander who is aware that subordinates or other persons under his control are going to commit or have committed a breach of the Convention or of the Protocol to initiate such steps as are necessary to prevent such violations and so forth. Your Honours, there is a basic proposition in international humanitarian law dealing with camp commanders and prison commanders, and that principle is set out very simply. It is that a prison commander such as Aleksovski has certain duties and responsibilities. These duties are not restricted solely to the physical maintenance of the prison or charges. It goes beyond that to create a positive and affirmative, as opposed to a passive, duty, to be responsible for the physical and mental well-being or health of the prisoners. The reason for this duty is clear. It is because the liberty of the prisoner has been taken away and that they cannot protect themselves that the commander is responsible for protecting them against attack, both within the prison and from outside. The civilian prisoners at Kaonik during the time that the accused was the commander were never charged with any crime. Nor was it asserted to international observers that they had committed any crime. It seems that the whole basis for their detention was their ethnicity. It was their Muslim ethnicity which determined whether or not they would be detained. Once detained, their continued detention was justified on the basis that they would be suitable for exchange. Thus these civilian prisoners were a bargaining chip for some future exchange. Your Honours, it is illegal to detain innocent civilians in order to have a store of human bargaining chips so that some future exchange might take place. It is inhumane and constitutes an outrage upon the personal dignity of the victim. Our evidence will show, your Honours, that the Muslim detainees were abused and mistreated not only by the prison guards, who were under the direct control and command of Aleksovski in a direct hierarchical line, but also by HVO troops. There is evidence that first HVO troops were allowed to enter the cells at night and abuse the prisoners. There is evidence that the HVO troops, with Aleksovski's knowledge and permission, took detainees to dig trenches under hazardous conditions. Your Honours, the accused Aleksovski had control over the keys to the cells of the prisoners. Prisoners around the world have one thing in common, in that the prisoners are locked up and the reason that they are locked up is because they will not escape, so when they are placed in cells and the keys turned, they cannot get out. But the converse is also true. When the key is turned and HVO troops with impunity enter the cells and abuse the prisoners, or when the key is turned and the prisoners are given to the HVO troops to abuse them as human shields or to use them against their will to force them to dig trenches in hazardous conditions, the common fact lies in control over the key; who had the key? Your Honours, the accused Aleksovski had control over the keys and when he chose to allow the key to be used, to have his prisoners that he was responsible for subjected to inhumane treatment, he either became a party to or failed to prevent the occurrences of inhumane treatment. Your Honour, our evidence will show that the accused Aleksovski demonstrated control and custody over the liberty of the detainees at Kaonik prison. Some examples of that are firstly when ECMM monitors went to Kaonik to observe the conditions, he suggested the -- and the ECMM monitor suggested the release of a particular prisoner, the accused Aleksovski, without seeking any advice, permission or orders from anyone, immediately released that detainee. This demonstrates that the accused Aleksovski, when he wanted to, had control over the liberty of detainees. Another example is an event where Aleksovski refused to comply with the request of an HVO commander to get prisoners to dig trenches. This demonstrates that Aleksovski had and in fact did exercise determination of whether or not the detainees could be taken by the HVO. The next element, your Honours, or the second element in proof of this is the issue of knowledge. Aleksovski knew or had information which would have enabled him to conclude that a breach was being committed, or was going to be committed, or had been committed. The elements may be established either through actual knowledge, established by direct or circumstantial evidence, or through establishing that the accused would have had knowledge were it not for his wilful blindness to the circumstances. The Prosecution submits, your Honour, that the mens rea standard has to be applied in the broader context of the far-reaching and comprehensive duty of military commanders to take all necessary measures to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law on the part of their subordinates. Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal provides that the accused, being in a position of superior responsibility, is responsible for a failure to act with respect to breaches of international humanitarian law committed by his subordinates. If he knew or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit such acts or had done so. Accordingly, knowledge of criminal acts committed by subordinates may be actual or constructive. In particular: "Ignorance does not absolve superiors from responsibility if it can be attributed to a fault on their part. The fact that breaches have widespread public notoriety, are numerous and occur over a long period and in many places, should be taken into consideration in reaching a presumption that the person responsible could not be ignorant of them." The Yamashita case indicates that the public notoriety of crimes can be a decisive factor in determining the knowledge of the accused. I quote from that decision where their Honours said: "Where murder and rape and vicious revengeful acts and widespread offences and there is no effective attempt by a commander to discover or control the criminal acts, such a commander may be held responsible, even criminally liable for lawless acts of his troops, depending upon their nature and circumstances surrounding them." Furthermore, the Tribunal in the German High Command trial attributed criminal responsibility to a superior: "Where his failure to properly supervise his subordinates constitutes criminal negligence on his part ... It must be a personal neglect amounting to wanton, immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates, amounting to acquiescence." Accordingly, the requisite mens rea under Article 7(3) exists if the accused either possessed actual knowledge of the violations established through direct evidence or through circumstantial evidence with a presumption of knowledge where the crimes of the subordinates are a matter of public notoriety, are numerous, occur over a prolonged period or in a wide geographical area, or if the accused wantonly disregarded information of a general nature within his reasonable access, indicating the likelihood of actual and prospective criminal conduct on the part of his subordinates. Your Honours, our evidence regarding mistreatment of detainees will show that prisoners were being kept in cramped or crowded conditions, for example men were cramped in cells for long periods of time. The accused Aleksovski had knowledge of these conditions, he admitted it to ECMM monitors, an observer who visited the camp, that he realised the facilities were poor and said that the facilities were in fact not built for the purpose. Another example is of a man placed in these cells was given one blanket to share between two men. This was at a period of time when the camp would get so cold that in fact the temperatures ranged from minus 10 degrees Celsius. Another kind of mistreatment your Honours will hear about is inadequate food. The men were fed one or two times over a 24-hour period. These men were often called upon to do hard physical labour and needed nutrition and they were given rations that were not enough for one man and yet they were forced to share inadequate rations between two. The accused, of his own admission to the ECMM monitors, acknowledged that the food supplies were inadequate. A third type of misconduct that occurred at the prison itself was inadequate or no medical care. In fairness to Mr. Aleksovski and certainly in comparison to what we have seen in other camps, the Prosecution concedes that he did show some concern for the prisoners. It is true and to his credit that medical care was supplied to some of the prisoners, but the reality is equally that there were occasions when people needed medical care and were given none, or were given inadequate medical care. The fourth kind of mistreatment in Kaonik prison that the Prosecution will bring evidence of is physical and psychological abuse. These abuses took place in the setting of prolonged interrogations where brute force was brought to bear on prisoners who had nowhere to run or escape. The Muslim detainees were constantly abused, intimidated and psychologically tortured. The beatings occurred mostly at night. Many of the witnesses will speak of the screams that occurred throughout the night. Your Honours, Aleksovski knew of the beatings and the physical abuse that the detainees under his protection were subjected to. Aleksovski admitted as much to ECMM officials, that he knew the guards beat the prisoners, and even goes on to explain why they may have done that. Last but not least, our evidence may show that Aleksovski had actual knowledge of Muslim detainees being forced to dig trenches; in fact our evidence will show that Aleksovski maintained lists of detainees from which prisoners were selected for trench digging. Aleksovski freely admitted his knowledge that civilians were being sent to dig trenches when questioned by international observers. Not only did Aleksovski know of the fact that Muslim detainees were being sent to dig trenches, he also knew that there was an inherent danger in digging trenches on the front-line. He knew that these trenches were on the confrontation lines and were dangerous, he knew that his own HVO, the Croats were getting killed while digging trenches, so he knew about the possibility of Muslim people being killed there as well. Furthermore, Aleksovski knew that some of these detainees never came back from trench digging. Our evidence will show that the beatings, physical abuse of the detainees was so widespread in Kaonik that he had abundant constructive knowledge of the matters and of the manner in which his subordinates were mistreating the detainees. The testimony will show that his office was in the same building where the detainees were physically abused. Your Honours, Article 3(1) of the fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 clearly states that: "No physical or moral coercion shall be exercised against protected persons, in particular to obtain information from them or from third parties." Article 3(2) provides that: "The high contracting parties specifically agree each of them is prohibited from taking any matters of such a character to cause the physical suffering, extermination of protected persons in their hands. This prohibition applies not only to murder, torture, corporal punishment, mutilation, medical and scientific experiments, not necessarily suited for medical treatment of a protected person, but also to any other measures of brutality, whether applied by civilian or military agents." Moreover, the accused Aleksovski also knew that detainees had to be handed over to the HVO for trench digging and were subjected to physical abuse when doing that. Many of them returned to the camp after having been to the trenches with visible injuries. Your Honours, Article 40 of the fourth Geneva Convention, dealing with civilians, the second paragraph specifically provides: "If protected persons of enemy nationality, they may only be compelled to do work which is normally necessary to ensure the feeding, sheltering, clothing, transport and health of human beings and which is not directly related to the conduct of military operations." Article 95 provides that: "The detaining power shall not employ internees as workers unless they so desire and any employment in which they are so engaged shall not be of a degrading or humiliating character." Your Honours, what emerges from the above discussion is that the accused Aleksovski clearly was on notice and had knowledge, actual knowledge of the mistreatment of the detainees under his protection and control, yet he did not take all of the necessary preventative measures under his control to improve the situation for the hapless detainees. Our evidence will show, your Honours, that by denying prisoners basic conditions, safeguarding health or hygiene, not providing them with adequate clothing according to the climate is a breach of the Geneva Conventions. Article 85, for example, of the fourth Geneva Convention requires that: "... detainees be accommodated in buildings or quarters which afford possible safeguards as regards hygiene and health. The premises shall be protected against dampness, adequately heated and lit. Internees shall be given suitable bedding, sufficient blankets suitable for the climate. Internees shall have the use day and night of sanitary conveniences which conform to the rules of hygiene, and are constantly maintained in the state of cleanliness. They should be provided with sufficient water and soap for their daily toilet", et cetera. Article 89 provides that: "Daily rations for internees shall be sufficient in quantity and variety to keep them in a good state of health and further that internees who work shall receive additional rations in proportion to the kind of labour they perform." Article 90 provides that: "Internees shall be given all the facilities to provide themselves with necessary clothing, footwear", and so forth. In addition to that, under Article 91: "There shall be in a place of internment an adequate infirmary under the direction of a qualified doctor where internees may have the attention they require for their medical needs." All of these, your Honours, are provided for clearly and specifically in the Geneva Conventions and in our submission, your Honours, all of these are recognised in their abuse at the Kaonik centre. The next element, your Honours, that I deal with is prevention of punishment. The evidence will show that the accused Aleksovski failed to take necessary and reasonable steps to prevent such acts or to prohibit the perpetrators who committed them. One detainee who will testify was beaten frequently, sometimes for most of the day, and was one of the victims among many that Aleksovski failed to attend to, or to take action in relation to. This detainee reports a conversation between a prison guard, who went to Aleksovski and said, "did you not promise me that this detainee would not leave the camp alive?"; Aleksovski replied, "can you see his condition? He will not survive and it is better that they will die in their hands than in ours". Moreover, according to this witness, the beatings increased after he had complained, and ultimately he was assured by Aleksovski that he would be beaten no more. Clearly such statements indicate that Aleksovski had notice and knowledge of grave violations and once having notice and knowledge, he failed to either prevent the reoccurrence of such acts or failed to punish those who perpetrated the acts. Thus the Prosecution submits that by disregarding the well-being of the detainees, Zlatko Aleksovski failed to act in accordance with his duty towards the detainees. Under customary international law, a commander is under an obligation to ensure that persons under his command are aware of their obligations to abide by the provisions of international law and they must do so either periodically or expressly. We will present evidence to show that Aleksovski did issue some of these types of orders and thus did know of his responsibilities. However, the mere issuance of routine orders to abide by the Geneva Conventions does not relieve a commander of criminal responsibility. His concomitant duty is to ensure that his orders are being effectively carried out. The commander has an affirmative duty to take all necessary measures for the protection of the civilian population. As was stated in the Hostages Case, and I quote: "The primary responsibility for the prevention and punishment of crime lie with the commander general, a responsibility that he cannot escape by denying authority over the perpetrators. Notably the duty of commanders to acquire knowledge concerning the actions of their subordinates includes the establishment and securing of an effective functioning reporting system." The requirement was set forth by the international military tribunal for the Far East in a part of its decision dealing with war crimes against prisoners and they said as follows: "It is the duty of all those on whom responsibility rests to secure proper treatment of prisoners and to prevent their ill-treatment by establishing and securing the continuous and efficient working of an appropriate system for these purposes. Such persons fail in this duty and become responsible for ill-treatment of prisoners if they fail to establish such a system or if, having established such a system, they fail to secure its continued and efficient working. A military commander has a duty to ascertain that the system is working and if he neglects to do so, he is responsible. He does not discharge his duty by merely instituting an appropriate system and thereafter neglecting to learn of its application. Furthermore, even if "a proper system and its continuous efficient functioning be provided for", in addition to actual knowledge that such crimes were being committed, military commanders may be held responsible if: "... they are at fault in having failed to acquire such knowledge. If such a person had or should but for negligent or supineness have had such knowledge, he is not excused for an action if his office required or permitted him to take any action to prevent such crimes. "On the other hand, it is not enough for the exculpation of a person otherwise responsible for him to show that he accepted assurances from others more directly associated with the control of prisoners if having regard to the position of those others to the frequency or reports of such crimes, or to the circumstances he should have been put upon further enquiry as to whether those assurances were true or untrue; that crimes are notorious, numerous and widespread as to the time, place and matters are to be considered in imputing knowledge." In view of the more exacting standards imposed on military superiors, it is instructive to consider the dictum of the French Superior Military Court on the defence of lack of knowledge in the trial of the directors of the firm Roechling, involving in part the more limited superior responsibility of civilian industrialists for criminal acts of their subordinates. No superior may prefer this defence indefinitely, for it is his duty to know what occurs in his organisation and lack of knowledge therefore can only be the result of criminal negligence. For the rest, the acceptance of superior orders on the one hand and the lack of knowledge as to the execution by subordinates on the other would lead to the abolishment of any penalty, the executing agents would seek cover behind the superior orders and the superior behind his lack of knowledge and say, "I had no knowledge of that". It is in light of this well-established jurisprudence that the standard of "knew or had information" should have enabled him to conclude in the circumstances at the time. Your Honours, in Article 86(2) of the 1977 Additional Protocol of the Geneva Conventions, it is provided there that the breach of the Convention or the Protocol -- the fact that the breach of the Convention or the Protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility, as the case may be, if they knew or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time that he was committing or was going to commit such a breach, or if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress such brief. In its commentary to the draft Code of Crimes Against the Peace and Security of Mankind, the International Law Commission notes that: "The phrase 'had reason to know' contained in the provision on responsibility of the superior corresponding to Article 6 is taken from the statutes of the tribunals on Rwanda and Yugoslavia and should be understood as having the same meaning as 'had information enabling them to conclude' which is used in Additional Protocol 1." The Commission decided to use the former phrase to ensure an objective rather than subjective interpretation of the mens rea standard. The Commission states furthermore that the "had information enabling them to conclude" standard of Protocol 1 simply means that the superior has sufficient relevant information to enable him to conclude under the circumstances of the time that his subordinates are committing or about to commit a crime. In this situation, a superior does not have to have actual knowledge of the unlawful conduct being planned or perpetrated by his subordinates, but he has sufficient relevant information of a general nature that would enable him to conclude that this is the case. With respect to the affirmative duty to know, the Commission states that a superior who simply ignores information which clearly indicates the likelihood of criminal conduct on the part of his subordinates is seriously negligent in failing to perform his duty to prevent or suppress such conduct by failing to make a reasonable effort to obtain the necessary information that will enable him to take appropriate action. Although this category of knowledge is in our submission sufficient for the accused to be found guilty, our evidence in this case will show that Aleksovski had actual knowledge. Yet despite the knowledge of the crimes committed by his subordinates, he failed to take the necessary measures to suppress breaches or to punish his subordinates. Indeed, our evidence will go further and will show that Aleksovski participated himself in some of these egregious acts. According to one detainee, Aleksovski never prevented the beating and that the soldiers involved were never punished. His preventative actions, half-hearted commands at best, did not have any deterrent effects. This detainee heard Aleksovski give a command to watch the prisoners more carefully and not to beat them so much. Clearly this statement shows that Aleksovski knew about the beatings and mistreatment of prisoners, but his concern for their well-being was limited to a degree of mistreatment, rather than preventing the mistreatment from happening at all. Moreover, the accused Aleksovski allowed Muslim detainees to be forced to dig trenches in hazardous conditions. Justice and international standards of command responsibility cannot be defined at such a low threshold that a half-hearted attempt to control atrocities will suffice. To do so would be to make a travesty of the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions which were framed precisely for preventing such occurrences. The commander has a duty to do everything in his power to protect the detainees, especially civilians under his control. Superiors are under a duty to take all measures within their power in accordance with the means at their disposal to prevent or punish breaches of humanitarian law. In particular, Protocol 1 stipulates that superiors are obligated to undertake a wide range of measures to prevent and punish subordinate perpetrators. As the International Committee of the Red Cross commentary to Protocol 1 points out, the role of the commander is decisive, whether they are concerned with the theatre of military operations, occupied territories or places of internment, the necessary measures for the proper application of the Conventions and the Protocols must be taken at the level of the troops so that a fatal gap between the undertakings entered into by parties to the conflict and the conduct of individuals is avoided. At this level, everything depends on commanders and without their conscious supervision, general legal requirements are likely to be affected. Article 87 of Protocol 1, which I referred to earlier, obligates commanders to firstly prevent and, where necessary, suppress and report to the competent authority breaches of the Geneva Conventions in Protocol 1. Secondly, to take measures to ensure that armed forces under their command are aware of their obligations. In specific terms, the duty of a commander in taking the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish violations of the humanitarian law is dealt with again in the International Committee of the Red Cross's commentary when it says: "It is not a matter of transferring to military commanders the competence and responsibilities which are those of the judicial authority. Even if it is a military court, whether or not it is represented by a military commission constituted in accordance with the law, the object of these texts is to ensure that military commanders at every level exercise the power vested in them, both with regard to the provisions of the Conventions and the Protocols and with regard to other rules of the army to which they belong. Such powers exist in all armies. They may concern at any level informing superior officers of what is taking place in the sector, drawing up a report in case of a breach, intervening with a view to preventing a breach from being committed, proposing a sanction to a superior who has disciplining power or, in the case of someone who holds such power himself, exercising it within the limits of his competence; and finally remitting the case to judicial authorities where necessary with such factual evidence as is possible to find." It is thus evident that various superiors at the same and different levels in hierarchy can be legally responsible to prevent or to punish the unlawful acts of some subordinates. The failure of any such superior to fulfil his duties in this regard cannot excuse another superior's failure to undertake necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances. The obligations of superiors apply in the context of responsibilities as they have devolved over different levels of hierarchy, within the confines of each of the areas of competence. The responsibility of each of these applies with respect to all of the members of the armed forces under the superior's command. Under Article 7(3) of the Statute, the superior's duty to punish subordinate extends to violations that were committed before the superior was appointed if he knew or should have known about these violations after he assumed command of the perpetrators. In the event that the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators in these circumstances, he can be held criminally liable for the violations committed by his subordinates. In the German High Command trial, Field Marshall von Keschler was held responsible for the illegal execution of red army soldiers which occurred before he took up command, on the basis that the reports of these executions were made to his headquarters and he took up command and he took no punitive action in relation thereto. Finally, in determining the accused took the necessary and reasonable measures, where a commander acted pursuant to an order of a superior, Article 7(4) of the Statute clearly provides that he shall not be relieved of criminal responsibilities. Your Honours, as principal commander, Aleksovski met with international officials, provided them with lists of detained persons and acknowledged his position in the facility. He demonstrated an understanding of the Geneva Conventions. He knew that civilians were being sent out to dig trenches, yet he did not ensure the well-being of the detainees whom he had the duty to protect. He did not give any orders countermanding the illegal orders of forcing civilians to dig trenches. He did not resign, he did not report the matter to any competent authority. There is no evidence that he tried to distance himself from what he knew to be illegal. There is no evidence that he said, "I am abhorred by what is going on and I resign". In summary, under the doctrine of superior responsibility, incorporated in Article 7(3) of the Statute, the accused Aleksovski, as camp commander of Kaonik prison, is criminally responsible for the violations of international humanitarian law committed by his subordinates over whom he has direct or indirect command and control, whether exercised de jure or de facto, Aleksovski knew or had reason to know, which includes ignorance resulting from superior's failure to properly supervise his subordinates that these acts were about to be committed or even had been committed. The superior liability of Aleksovski arises on the basis that a superior is under a duty to take all reasonable or necessary measures. Your Honours, our evidence will show that Aleksovski failed to discharge this duty. Your Honours, I note the time and I am now about to pass on to that aspect of the case relating to international armed conflict. Might it be a suitable time for us to have a break now?
