utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, I will now move on to discuss the issue of international armed conflict, and then some other minor matters and then my opening will be complete. Your Honours, Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal is applicable when the following legal elements are satisfied. Firstly, the existence of an international armed conflict or occupation between two or more internationally recognised states or de facto state entities. Two, the victims are protected under one or more of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the side of the international armed conflict to which the accused is linked, in particular in the 1949 Geneva Convention relative to the protection of civilian persons in time of war (Geneva Convention IV) protects civilians, while the 1949 Geneva Convention relative to the treatment of prisoners of war (Geneva Convention III) protects prisoners of war. Thirdly, that the accused committed one of the enumerated acts listed in Article 2 of the Statute. These elements are derived from the 1949 Geneva Conventions. The Appeals Chamber held that Article 2 of the Statute is based on the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and more specifically the provisions of those Conventions relating to the grave breaches. Article 2 of the Statute is therefore applicable to the present case where the requirements that render the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions operative are fulfilled. The Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case has decided that Article 2 of the Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of international conflict. Your Honours, we will provide evidence that an international armed conflict between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia existed during the period of time when the offences referred to in the indictment are alleged to have been committed. We will also demonstrate that the victims of the alleged offences were, for the purposes of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, protected persons linked to the Bosnian side of the conflict, while the alleged perpetrators had a nexus with the Bosnian Croat authorities and the Bosnian Croat entity was in fact linked to Croatia. The alleged offences are grave breaches because they are acts prohibited by the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions committed against protected persons on the Bosnian side of the international conflict by persons with a link to the Croatian side. Dealing firstly with international armed conflict, Article 2, common to all four of the Geneva Conventions, establishes the general applicability of the Conventions and as such Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Convention applies to all cases of declared war or any other armed conflict which may arise between two or more of the high contracting parties, even if a state of war is not recognised by one of them. The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a high contracting party. The high contracting parties are internationally recognised states, and accordingly the Appeals Chamber has held that: "In the present state of development of the law, Article 2 of the Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of international armed conflicts." The existence of international armed conflict is defined in the International Committee of the Red Cross's commentary on Geneva Convention IV in the following terms: "There is no need for a formal declaration of war, or the recognition of the state of war, as preliminaries to the application of the Convention. The occurrence of de facto hostilities is sufficient ... Any difference arising between two states and leading to the intervention of armed forces is an armed conflict within the meaning of Article 2, even if one of the parties denies the existence of a state of war. It makes no difference how long the conflict lasts, or how much slaughter takes place. The respect due to human persons as such is not measured by the number of victims." The Appeals Chamber adopted a similar view in finding that: "Armed conflict exists wherever there is resort to armed force between states ... International humanitarian law applies from the initiation of such armed conflicts and extends beyond cessation of hostilities until a general conclusion of peace is reached ... Until that moment international humanitarian law continues to apply in the whole of the territory of the warring states, whether or not actual combat takes place there." Furthermore, the Appeals Chamber confirmed the temporal and geographical requirements for the application of the Geneva Conventions by stating that: "The temporal and geographical scope of ... international armed conflict extends beyond the exact time and place of hostilities ... [for example]... each of the four Geneva Conventions contains language intimating their application beyond the cessation of hostilities." In particular, in terms of Article 6 of the Geneva Convention IV, the Convention will apply from the beginning of an international armed conflict until one year has elapsed after the general close of military operations. In terms of Article 5 of Geneva Convention III: "The present convention", that is Convention III, "shall apply to the persons referred to in Article 4 from the time they fall into the power of the enemy until their final release and repatriation. Should any doubt arise as to whether persons, having committed a belligerent act and having fallen into the hands of the enemy, belong to any of the categories enumerated in Article 4, such persons shall enjoy the protection of the present Convention until such time as their status has been determined by a competent tribunal." The Appeals Chamber further held that: "The grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions apply to the entire territory of the parties to the conflict, not just the vicinity of actual hostilities." Your Honours, it is submitted by the Prosecutor that an international armed conflict involving Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one hand, the Republic of Croatia and the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the other, occurred at a minimum during 1993 and early 1994. During this time, the army of Croatia, the HV, intervened and were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and were involved in an armed conflict with the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our evidence will demonstrate that in accordance with the requirements of Article 2 of the Geneva Convention, an international armed conflict existed due to these military interventions by one state, Croatia, into another state, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the existence of de facto hostilities, irrespective of whether any of the states involved recognised that a state of war existed between them. Further, our evidence will show that at least during 1993 the armed forces of the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Community of HB, were involved in an armed conflict with the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the Croatian Community of HB and the HVO were sufficiently related to Croatia and its armed forces, the HV, to be regarded as a component part of one side to the international armed conflict, namely Croatia, with the armed forces of another state, Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a result of this close political and military relationship, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO can be regarded as agents or as an extension of Croatia and of the Croatian army, the HV. It is significant to note at this juncture that both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were high contracting parties of the Geneva Conventions when the attack on the Lasva Valley area occurred, in that they had acceded to the four Geneva Conventions and to the two additional Protocols, on 11th May 1992 and on 31st December 1992 respectively. In addition, our evidence will demonstrate that the alleged attacks in the Lasva Valley area which form the background to the detention of the Muslim prisoners in Kaonik and the alleged commission of the offences with which the accused Zlatko Aleksovski was charged occurred in the course of this particular armed conflict. The attacks involved the same parties to the aforementioned conflict. It occurred during the same time that this conflict was taking place and on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Furthermore, the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, was linked to the Croatian side of the armed conflict and the victims, the Muslim detainees, to the Bosnia-Herzegovina side. Notably, the Appeals Chamber decision on jurisdiction in the Prosecutor v Tadic clearly stated that international humanitarian law applies from the beginning of the resort to armed force inter alia between states and extends beyond cessation of hostilities to the general conclusion, peace. Accordingly, the resort to armed force between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HV/HVO in Bosnia which commenced at least at the beginning of 1993 and concluded with the Washington Peace Agreement in March 1994, can be regarded as one international armed conflict, which included the attack on the Lasva Valley area. The law applicable to international armed conflict can therefore be applied to this attack. Other conflicts had preceded this conflict, and even continued during this conflict. In certain parts of Bosnia, for example, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was fighting against the Bosnian Serb Army, and in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO and the HV were involved in conflict against the Bosnian Serb Army, which at times also involved forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Appeals Chamber in the Tadic judgement has indicated its expectation that all potential victims will be treated equally. The Appeals Chamber in the decision on jurisdiction outlined the basic rules for classifying the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia. It concluded on the basis of interpreting the Statute that resolutions of the Security Council of the International Commission of the Red Cross agreements between the various parties to the conflict: "That the conflict in the former Yugoslavia have both internal and international aspects." The conflict: "Could have been characterised as both internal and international, or alternatively, as an internal conflict alongside an international one, or as an internal conflict that had become internationalised because of external support, or as an international conflict that had subsequently been replaced by one or more internal conflicts, or some combination thereof." The perpetrators and victims of violations in this area need not have participated in the planning, ordering or commission of the military involvement of one state in another which rendered the armed conflict international, or have intentionally or knowingly contributed to such involvement. The Appeals Chamber has stated that: "It is sufficient that the alleged crimes were closely related to the hostilities occurring in other parties of the territories controlled by the parties to the conflict." As discussed below, the Geneva Conventions are therefore applicable when the perpetrators and victims are recognisably linked to the different sides of the international armed conflict. The involvement of Croatia in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the relationship between Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna constitutes such a link. Notwithstanding what was said by the majority of the Trial Chamber in the Tadic case about international armed conflict, our view is that the test set down by the Trial Chamber II in the decision in the Rule 61 hearing of the Prosecutor v Rajic is the correct test to be applied, when it said: "This Chamber... is required to decide whether the Bosnian Croats can be regarded as agents of Croatia for establishing subject-matter jurisdiction over discrete acts which are alleged to be violations of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Specific operational control is therefore not critical to the inquiry. Rather, the Trial Chamber focuses on general political and military control exercised by Croatia over the Bosnian Croats." Accordingly, it is the submission of the Prosecutor that by applying this decision to the conflict involving Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in 1993 and early 1994, the conflict can be classified as international on the basis of the direct military involvement of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the existence of hostilities resulting therefrom, and the existence of hostilities between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which were very closely related to and controlled by Croatia and its armed forces. To the extent that the finding of the court on the required degree of control is to be regarded as an acceptable standard in accordance with the provisions of Rule 61, this standard has at least been satisfied in the Rule 61 hearing concerning Rajic. Croatia's involvement in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina through the intervention of its own forces and its close relationship with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna exhibits both the necessary degree of involvement and control to render the conflict international. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is closely related to Croatia. This relationship is different to the kind of relationship that existed between the United States and the Contra forces as was considered in the Nicaraguan case. In particular, the close political and military relationship between Croatia and the self-proclaimed Community of Herceg-Bosna has no parallel in the relationship between the United States and the Contras. These distinctions are manifest in numerous ways, including the fact that Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are governed by branches of the same political party, the HDZ. The Bosnian Croats are citizens of Croatia, Croatia controlled the political life of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and removed and replaced its political leaders, such as Mate Boban. Similarly, HV and HVO generals had been appointed, promoted and transferred by Croatia, and have acted on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in establishing the federation with Bosnia-Herzegovina in March 1994. Your Honours, our evidence will show that an international armed conflict existed on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all material times, on the basis that the HV and HVO was engaged in combat with the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces and that the HVO was under such degree of control by Croatia that it must be regarded as an agent of the Croatian government. The required level of control under international law for the purposes of applying grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions is not that Croatia should completely control the HVO, so that a shared unity of identity between the two can be established. Furthermore, in the case of the military and paramilitary activities in and against Nicaragua, to the extent that it is applicable, did not require the existence of unity of identity. Instead, the standard laid down was: "Whether the relationship was so much one of dependence on the one side and control on the other that it would be right to equate the Contras, for legal purposes, with an organ of the United States government, or as acting on behalf of that government." It is submitted by the Prosecution, your Honours, that the application of this rule to the conflict between Bosnia and Croatia and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna renders the conflict international. The presence of the armed forces of Croatia in BiH. The military intervention of the Croatian armed forces into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 and early 1994 and including the period of the attack on the Lasva Valley area is evidenced by various resolutions and reports of the United Nations. On 18th January 1993, the Secretary General noted that the earlier resolutions of the General Assembly demanding that Croatia withdraw its troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been observed. The statement by the President of the Security Council on 10th May 1993 called upon Croatia to adhere strictly to its obligations under Security Council Resolution 752 of 15th May 1992, that had demanded an end to all hostilities and interference in Bosnia-Herzegovina by elements of the Croatian army, but which had still not been fulfilled. The Secretary General's report of 1st February 1994 indicated that there were approximately 3,500 regular Croatian HV troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Security Council Presidential statement, issued on 3rd February 1994, strongly condemned Croatia for deploying elements of its army and heavy military equipment in central and southern parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and demanded that they be withdrawn. The Secretary General's report to the Security Council of 17th February 1994 noted that some 5,000 Croatian army troops remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina, despite the Council's demand for their withdrawal. The Secretary General's report of 16th March 1994 noted the continuing involvement of Croatia's army in central and southern Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of the aforementioned United Nations resolutions and reports explicitly and implicitly describe the nature of the HV, the Croatian military force's involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the context of condemning the HV's presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, certain explicit references were made to killing, torturing and illegally detaining Muslim civilians. The general hostilities between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were also mentioned and in this context specific attacks were reported, such as on Mostar and on Vitez. Furthermore, the location in Bosnia-Herzegovina where it is reported that HV troops were deployed, and the use of terms like "hostilities", "violence", "interference" and "violations of international humanitarian law", in the course of demanding the withdrawal of the HV from Bosnia-Herzegovina, imply that the HV was involved in an armed conflict with the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition, the conflict between the HV and various Serb forces are consistently reported separately from the involvement of the Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The United Nations resolutions and reports were preceded by numerous demands by the Security Council and General Assembly during 1992 for Croatia to withdraw its troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina. During this period, the HV and the HVO had united with the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces against the JNA and the Serb armed forces. The military alliance was short-lived as tensions between the various parties began to emerge as early as May 1992. During 1993, an armed conflict broke out between the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces and the closely aligned HV and HVO over the control of various territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which asserted their autonomy from BiH and allegiance to Croatia. On 16th April 1993, the HVO attacked the predominantly Muslim village of Ahmici, killing scores of unarmed civilians and destroying Muslim homes. On 9th May 1993, Mostar was attacked, and later fighting erupted in the municipalities of Stolac, Kiseljak, Busovaca, Capljina, Vitez and Novi Travnik. By 23rd February 1994, Croatia, the Bosnian Croats and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had signed a cease-fire agreement, and on 18th March 1994, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had entered into a confederation. Turning now to the political and military relationship between Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the very close political and military relationship between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and Croatia and the degree of control exercised by Croatia over the Croatian Community is evidenced in a variety of ways. From its inception, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna openly associated itself with Croatia. The Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, was the governing party in both Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The declaration on 18th November 1991 that established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna stated that the Bosnian Croats were in alliance with the HDZ ruling party of Croatia. The declaration designated seven municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. These municipalities encompassed the Herzegovinian region of Bosnia, which has historically been the focus of Croatian nationalism in Bosnia, being geographically and politically aligned to Croatia. Although one of the main stated reasons for the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was initially to defend Croats against Serbs and the JNA, the emphasis shifted during 1992 to the defence of Croatians living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This objective was reflective of emerging political policies at the highest levels. President Tudjman of Croatia, having initially recognised the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had stated publicly on a Zagreb radio broadcast on 6th July 1992 that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided into three constituent nations on a cantonal basis. His declaration had been preceded in early 1992 by the removal of Stjepan Klujic, a supporter of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was opposed to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina along ethnic lines, as the President of the HDZ of Bosnia. Klujic was replaced by Mate Boban, who supported Croatian involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This appointment laid the basis for the development of a very close political relationship during 1993 between the governments of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was centred on ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mate Boban was later to be removed from office by President Tudjman during the negotiations for the formation of a confederation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the beginning of 1994, only to be appointed by President Tudjman as director of the INA, a national oil company in Croatia. The very strong links between Croatia, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Bosnian Croats were manifest in the decision by Croatia to grant citizenship to all Bosnian Croats on 7th April 1992, when it recognised the existence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It entitles Bosnian Croats to the benefits of residence in Croatia and the right to vote in elections in Croatia, which they exercised in October 1995. Further, the level of control exercised by Croatia over the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was confirmed by the calls of the United Nations for President Tudjman to control activities of the Bosnian Croats and the HVO. The Secretary General's report of 30th April 1993 noted that President Tudjman had agreed to use his influence to ensure that those responsible for the acts of inhumanity which had occurred in Vitez be punished. The statement of the President of the Security Council of 10th May 1993 which called upon Croatia to withdraw troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina also called upon Croatia to exert all its influence on the Bosnian Croat leadership; to immediately cease attacks, particularly in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica. Again, the statement of the President of the Security Council of 14th September 1993, shortly before the attack on Stupni Do, asserted that the government of Croatia has a responsibility to use its influence with Bosnian Croats to secure compliance with Security Council demands concerning the treatment of detainees in detention camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These calls were reiterated by the many countries, including the United States, who demanded that Croatia suspend its support for the Bosnian Croats, following the attacks on the Muslim civilian population by the HVO. The Croatian government has also repeatedly acted on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in negotiating cease-fires and settlement agreements, including the Federation agreement between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was concluded on 18th March 1994. Similarly, the close association between the armed forces of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the substantial control the HV exerted over the HVO began when the HVO was created on 8th April 1992 as the supreme defence body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, with the stated objective of defending the Croatian population and culture in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Herzegovinian Croats in Croatia were instructed by the Croatian authorities to return and join the HVO. Many Croatian soldiers who were not born in Herzegovina also joined the HVO, although in most cases Croatian soldiers from Croatia all wore HVO, not HV insignia. This initiative developed from earlier relations between the two groupings and many Herzegovinian Croats had joined the police forces and the National Guard Corps in Croatia to defend Croatia against the Krajina Serbs during the armed conflict of 1990/1991. During 1992, a common campaign was waged by the HV and HVO to defend Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from the Serbs and the JNA. These close relations, and in particular the HV control over the HVO, were continued into the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least during 1993 and early 1994. As is evidenced by the above-mentioned United Nations resolutions and reports and the various other sources, the HV troops that were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the conflict with the Serb forces and the JNA were not withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They remained involved militarily during the conflict that emerged against the Bosnian armed forces, even though in many cases HV insignia were exchanged for those of the HVO. Confirmation of the HV's continued intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina is evidenced by the Secretary General's report of 1st February 1994, where it indicated that the HV had been directly supporting the HVO with manpower, equipment and weapons for some time. The number of HV soldiers had apparently increased, following successful offensives of the Bosnian government forces against the HVO. It was assessed that there was approximately 3,000 to 5,000 forces. To the extent to which the HVO is to be regarded as part of the HV is illustrated by the various appointments and transfers between the two armies. The HVO was both the Bosnian Croat army and the Bosnian Croat administration. During the relevant period, the HVO chief of staff or army commander was General Petkovic, an HV army officer from Croatia. During the relevant period, Goojko Susak, the Croatian Minister of Defence, exercised effective control over the HVO and General Petkovic; and General Praljak, the HV General from Croatia, also exercised control over HV forces. The Croatian government openly supported the activities of the HVO. On 14th March 1994, President Tudjman of Croatia signed the Washington Agreement with President Izetbegovic and the Bosnian Croat leader Zubakehic, which resulted in the Bosnian Croat Muslim federation. On 1st February 1995, General Martin Spegelj, former chief of the Croatian armed forces, said the war against the Muslims cost Croatia 3 million Deutschmarks per day. In an earlier statement in 1993, he said Croatia had sent more weaponry into Bosnia than it had retained in Croatia. In late 1994 for example, the HVO General, Petkovic, was moved to the post of HV commander in Osijek, and in November 1995, General Blaskic, the commander of the HVO, was appointed as Inspector in the general inspection of the HV by President Tudjman. To summarise, your Honours, the basis for the Prosecution's submission that Croatia was engaged in international armed conflict with Bosnia at the relevant time is firstly that the Croatian armed forces, the HVO, were engaged in combat with Bosnian armed forces in Bosnia, and secondly that the Bosnian Croat entity was under such a degree of control by Croatia that it must be regarded as an arm or agent of the Croatian government. The Prosecution will provide evidence for the position that Croatia controlled the Bosnian Croats and hence demonstrate that Croatia had its armed forces, the HV, be regarded as a component part of one side of the international armed conflict when it was in conflict with the other part, namely Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next requirement is that: "The offences under Article 2 can only be prosecuted when perpetrated against persons who are properly regarded as 'protected' by the Geneva Conventions under the conditions set out by the Conventions themselves." Article 4 of the Geneva Convention IV defines protected persons as: "Those who, at a given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves in the case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power of which they are not nationals." Article 4 of Geneva Convention III defines prisoners of war who must be protected as: "Prisoners of war, in the sense that they are persons belonging to one of the following categories who have fallen into the power of the enemy: "(1) members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict as well as members of militias or volunteer corps." Also, members of other militias or other volunteer corps belonging to a party operating in or outside their own territory, provided that certain conditions are met: such that they are commanded, they have distinctive signs, they carry arms openly and that they conduct their operations according to the laws and customs of war, and members of regular armed forces who profess allegiance to a government or authority not recognised by the detaining power. The Prosecution evidence will demonstrate that the victims in the present case were protected persons either under Article 4 of Geneva Convention III or Article 4 of Geneva Convention IV in that they were either prisoners of war or they were civilians. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that grave breaches must take place during an international armed conflict. Furthermore, the accused must be associated with one side of the international conflict, whereas the victims must be protected. Accordingly, they, the victims, have to be linked to the other party involved in the international armed conflict. In the present case, the requirements entail Bosnia-Herzegovina being one party and Croatia, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna closely related to and under the control of Croatia, being the other. The Prosecutor submits that the grave breaches with which the accused Aleksovski is charged occurred during this international armed conflict. Several of the Muslim victims who were unlawfully contained and mistreated at the Kaonik prison are protected persons in that they are civilians who were connected on the basis of the Bosnian nationality to the Bosnia-Herzegovina side of the conflict, and they were in the hands of the other party to the conflict. The International Committee of the Red Cross commentary on the Geneva Convention states that: "The expression 'in the hands of' is used in an extremely general sense ... the expression ... need not necessarily be understood in the physical sense; it simply means that the person is in territory under the control of the power in question." Accordingly, the civilian victims became protected persons when they came under the control of the HVO forces in the Lasva Valley area and were forcibly transferred to Kaonik prison under the command of Zlatko Aleksovski. The punishable grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions are listed in Article 130 of the third convention and include wilful killing, torture, inhumane treatment, wilfully causing great suffering and wilfully causing serious injury to body and health. Article 147 of the Geneva Convention IV also lists these acts as grave breaches. Your Honours, our evidence will show that at least some of the detainees were civilians and that they were non-combatants belonging to Bosnia-Herzegovina who had fallen into the hands of the HV/HVO and were clearly not members of the other party to the conflict, namely Croatia. In particular, they had not taken up arms, were not carrying arms openly during the military operations concerned. Many of them were unarmed and surrendered immediately upon the advance of the HVO Armed Forces. Accordingly, they cannot be regarded as prisoners of war under Geneva Convention III, but are protected civilians by Article 4 of Geneva Convention IV. All of the victims in this case are protected under various provisions of international humanitarian law which are embodied in Articles 2 and 3 of the Statute with which the accused has been charged. There is no conceivable situation in which the victims in the present case are not protected by rules of international humanitarian law which are punishable under the Statute of the Tribunal. There is a wide spectrum of applications under international humanitarian law that cover the victims in the present case. If one of them does not apply to the victims or a certain group of them, another will be applicable. Finally, your Honours, dealing with protection under Article 3 of the Statute, the victims are also protected under Article 3. A violation of Article 3 of the Statute is to breach the rules contained in common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, which apply during all armed conflicts, whether international or internal. The Appeals Chamber in its decision on the Defence motion for interlocutory appeals on jurisdiction in the Tadic decision on jurisdiction held that: "At least with respect to the minimum rules of common Article 3, the character of the conflict is irrelevant." The provisions of common Article 3 are as follows, that in the case of an armed conflict not of an international character, persons taking no part in the activities, and it lists them there, fall under the general protection of that provision and then specifically, the following acts are deemed to always remain prohibited: violence to life, the taking of hostages, outrages upon personal dignity and the passing of a sentence, in circumstances other than by a regularly constituted court. Accordingly, during any armed conflict, the victims in the present case are protected by these provisions in circumstances related to the armed conflict, if they do not take part in hostilities, from the moment they are no longer to take part in hostilities, irrespective of their nationality. Furthermore, during an international armed conflict, the nationals of the detaining power are protected by Article 75 of Additional Protocol 1, 1977. This protocol is applicable to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ratified the Geneva Conventions in 1950 and the additional protocols on 11th June 1979. Bosnia-Herzegovina acceded to the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols on 31st December 1992, and these accessions were backdated to its asserted date of independence, 6th March 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded the SFRY. The Vienna Convention on Succession of States in Respect of Treaties states in Article 34(1)(a) that: "Any treaty in force at the date of succession of states in respect of the entire territory of the predecessor state continues in force in respect of each successor state." Although this Convention is not in force, it reflects, in our submission, customary international law. Article 75 of Additional Protocol 1 1997 is similar in its prohibitions in relating to what can and cannot be done with people that fall into the hands of a party to the conflict. Violations of this provision are covered by Article 3 of the Statute in accordance with the Appeals Chamber's decision in its decision on jurisdiction on Article 3 when it said: "Article 3 is a general clause covering all violations of international humanitarian law not falling under Article 2 or covered by Articles 4 or 5, more specifically: ... (ii) infringements of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions other than those classified as 'grave breaches' ... (iv) violations of agreements binding upon the parties to the conflict, qua treaty law." In this regard, it is important to note that the International Committee of the Red Cross commentary refers to Article 75 as a: "'Mini Convention' ... which will certainly facilitate the dissemination of humanitarian law and the promulgation of its fundamental principles." In addition, the other leading commentary on the protocols states: "In all cases, Article 75 has to be applied to a Party's own nationals if they have acted in favour of the adversary and are made responsible for such acts by the authorities of their own state ... a highly important field of application of the minimum guarantees would arise when a civil war is connected with an international armed conflict and the nationals of a State are joining the forces of both sides." Your Honours, with respect to possible defences that may be raised in this case, at the outset it should be noted that no specific defences are listed in the Statute, but the Secretary General's report commenting on Article 7 of the Statute at paragraph 58 states: "The International Tribunal itself will have to decide on various personal defences which may relieve a person of individual criminal responsibility, drawing upon general principles of law." This statement is applicable to all possible defences that might be raised by the Defence. In accordance with the International Law Commission's Draft Code of Crimes Against the Peace and Security of Mankind, which provides in Article 14 that: "The competent court shall determine the admissibility of defences in accordance with the general principles of law in the light of the character of each crime." The Commentary on this provision notes that there are two criteria which must be taken into account when making the determination as to whether a defence is permissible: "First, the court must consider the validity of the defence raised by the accused under general principles of law. This first criterion limits the possible defences to those defences that are well established and widely recognised as admissible with respect to similarly serious crimes under national or international law. Second, the court must consider the applicability of the defence to the crime with which the accused is charged, in light of the character of the crime." It is submitted, your Honours, that these factors should be taken into account when determining whether any of the possible defences that may be raised by the Defence are valid. Your Honours, the accused Aleksovski's statements to date do not indicate any defences. He never acted or even claimed to have acted under superior orders or duress. He never disagreed or gave the impression to disagree with his superior orders; he did not feel uneasy in his role or distance himself from what he knew to be violations of the Geneva Conventions. He acknowledged his responsibilities. Your Honours, in the event that it is determined that the defence of duress, for example, whether in the context of superior orders or not, could constitute a defence, other than when it involves the killing of innocent human beings, the evidence presented by the Prosecutor in this case will clearly demonstrate that the accused does not satisfy the strict requirements of this defence. It is to no avail that the extent of the violations which did occur in the camp while the accused Aleksovski was commander were less than the detainees might have been exposed to if he had not been the commander. Zlatko Aleksovski is a professional, he has a sociology degree, he was active in the penal system in the former Yugoslavia before he took over as commander of the Kaonik prison. He may contend that when he arrived in Kaonik he brought his professional skills and expertise, and attempted to clean up the camp. His defence could be that he did everything within his powers to control and improve the circumstances of the prisoners; presumably he could say that the detainees would have been in a worse position if he had not been there. To the extent, your Honours, that the accused Aleksovski might argue that he had no choice but to remain in command of the camp and that he did all in his power in the circumstances to avoid endangering the detainees, it is submitted, your Honours, that this is in direct conflict with the evidence, it is speculative and is not made out. It is submitted that none of the violations, or the failure to prevent or punish them, alleged in the present indictment can be justified on the grounds that they prevented some greater harm occurring which has not been specified. No choice of evils existed and the crimes committed were certainly not lesser evils. Your Honours, in conclusion, I have gone to some lengths to set out the law as it applies to this case. The case is of a more narrow focus than other cases that have come before this Tribunal, and in some respects, the crimes that will be dealt with are not as egregious or widespread as may have occurred in other cases that have come before this Tribunal. I am sure that once you have heard all the evidence, you will have no doubt in finding the accused guilty as charged. The Prosecution evidence will clearly prove all of the elements of the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. War in any of its manifestations is evil. It is the curse of mankind that darkens our very existence. Struggle as we may, we cannot seem to rid ourselves of this horror. However, for our purposes, war is not illegal, so with that issue we are not concerned. What can be illegal, however, is what occurs during the course of war. If we cannot outlaw war then no doubt the next best thing is to control how war is waged. Therefore, in our submission, we should be vigilant to apply what law we have to ameliorate the agony of this odium. We urge your Honours to extend to this accused all that is fair and just in order that he might receive a fair trial, but at the same time we ask you not to lose sight of the suffering that has been inflicted upon the innocent victims of this crime. Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, I mentioned in the course of my address, and draw your Honours' attention to certain maps which may assist your Honours if I was to make them available to you, so at this stage or immediately before we commence -- I could do it now or later, but they are available to be tendered to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has no questions regarding the maps as we are familiar with the contents of these maps, we were familiarised with them before the beginning of trial.

utterances.text: I am indebted to my friend, your Honours. I will tender those maps now. I believe they have been made available to the Registrar. We have also made them available to your Honours for your Honours to have a personal copy.

utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. I was about to ask the Defence whether they intend to make an opening statement now or in the afternoon after lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We can now resume our hearing, and give the floor to Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. First of all, allow me to say good afternoon to all of you at the beginning of this trial, and to voice my gratitude that the trial started even a little earlier than we had originally expected. The Defence, pursuant to the provisions of Article 84 of the Rules of Procedure, Rule 84, avails itself of its right to speak in connection with the impending trial, and this opening statement will be shorter than was that of my learned colleague, the Prosecutor. The Defence wishes to thank our learned colleague the Prosecutor for the obvious effort made in his opening statement to specify certain facts linked to the actual indictment. Your Honours, the statement of the Defence may perhaps be rather unusual as compared to what is usually expected, but this is due to the fact which the Defence wishes to draw attention to, since the very initial appearance of this accused before the Trial Chamber. As has already been underlined, it is the view of the Defence that the indictment suffers from serious shortcomings which are not of a formal but of a substantive nature. Among those, it is particularly worth underlining that the indictment does not specify those facts which would be relevant with regard to the possible responsibility of the accused, nor those facts which would be relevant with regard to the form and the degree of the alleged culpability of the accused. It is the position of the Defence that the accused's behaviour has not been described in detail, the kind of behaviour that would entail criminal responsibility. In the desire to avoid repeating the substantive positions of the Defence regarding the charges which were elaborated in the motion of 19th June 1997, on this occasion the Defence counsel would like to highlight in particular the fact that the accused had, from the beginning ab initio been placed in an unequal position with regard to his fundamental rights guaranteed by the Statute, and specifically Article 21, paragraph 4(B) and (C) of the Statute, which states, and allow me to remind your Honours of this Article, that the accused must have sufficient time and facilities for the preparation of his Defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing, and that he has to be tried without undue delay. Proceeding from this, the Defence counsel wishes to draw attention to the fact that the accused in the realisation of these rights was not in a position to organise his Defence in an adequate manner, for the simple reason that the indictment itself did not indicate any specific criminal behaviour or offences because the indictment was drafted in generalised terms and without specifying individual criminal offences. However, the Defence certainly expects in the course of the trial proceedings themselves and the evidence that will be presented by the Prosecution that the generalised incriminations will be individualised, or that the Prosecution will act in accordance with the provisions of Rule 51 of the Rules of Procedure, and withdraw the indictment against the accused. The Defence will insist on the principle, and rigorous implementation of the principle, of direct evidentiary material as the generally accepted legal standard for an objective trial, and will emphatically oppose any attempt to apply analogy with the aim of proving certain facts which might be relevant for the possible responsibility of the accused. In any event, the Defence will, in its case, when presenting evidence in favour of the accused, will without any doubt prove that the accused is not responsible for any one of the counts in the indictment. The Defence counsel sincerely believes that it will be in a position to persuade your Honours of the innocence of the accused, but on condition that it has the possibility to respect the fundamental rights of the accused which are envisaged not only by the Statute of this Tribunal but which are generally accepted in the legal norms of civilised society. One of those fundamental rights of the accused is certainly the right to complete an unlimited, and I underline the word unlimited, communication with his Defence counsel, in the interest of preparing the Defence. Allow me to remind you and refer to Rule 67 regarding the Rules of Detention, which indicates that every suspect will have the right to complete and unlimited communication with his Defence counsel. Unfortunately, this fundamental right of the accused has been seriously impaired by the decision of the authorities of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, pursuant to which, the Defence counsel is not allowed access to the detention facilities of the United Nations after 5.00 pm. This situation illustrates the fact that the Defence counsel, after the completion of the hearing in court, is simply unable to contact his client to summarise the evidence presented and to engage in preparations for the next day of hearings. This, of course, is not possible the following morning of the next day of hearings, because again no access is allowed to the detention facility before 8.00 am, and after that time, the accused is brought to the premises of the Tribunal. Therefore, the Defence counsel does not have a chance in the course of the trial days to have any contact with his client except for a few minutes in the breaks during the actual hearings. Such a situation quite obviously limits and even undermines the fundamental right to unlimited communication with the defendant in the interests of the preparation of the Defence. The Defence counsel wishes to recall that the United Nations detention facility was established as an instrument of this Tribunal and that in that capacity, the Tribunal, or rather the Trial Chamber, is fully authorised to use its authority in order to protect the rights of the accused. I wish to remind your Honours of Rule 2 of the Rules of Detention, which states all detainees under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal, throughout their period of detention, and the director of the detention facility is also under the authority of the Tribunal and that he is the only one responsible for all aspects of detention. I remind Rule 3 of those Rules of Detention, it says that a team of experienced inspectors will be formed who will ensure management of detention in accordance with the Rules and will protect the individual rights of the detainees, and in this context, the right to unlimited contact with the accused is particularly underlined. The Defence has no doubts regarding the highest legal standards that are being applied in this Tribunal, and which will certainly in future be applied in this Trial Chamber as well, and for this very reason, and primarily in order to protect the fundamental rights of the accused to unhindered communication with his counsel, the Defence on this occasion expects, proposes and requests that your Honours, the members of this Trial Chamber, should without any further delay ensure the implementation and observance of the mentioned rights of the accused in accordance with Rule 6 of the principles that we have just cited. The Defence is aware of the complexity of the situation we have referred to, the ultimate outcome of which is a substantive limitation of the rights of the accused, but the Defence would like to underline that any further prolongation of the status quo constitutes a further lack of respect for the rights of the accused. Defence counsel views that this problem, in spite of all efforts by the Trial Chamber, will not lend itself to a prompt solution. Nevertheless, the public hearing has started and in view of the circumstance of the limited right of the accused to have unlimited contact with his counsel, due to this and not only because of this, the Defence counsel today in this courtroom and before this respected Trial Chamber, and referring to Article 65 of the Rules of Procedure, wishes to make a request for the provisional release of the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski, and this request will be argued by my learned co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, continuing where my colleague left off, I would like to say that the intention of the Defence in any event was to come up with this proposal, taking into account the fact -- the problem raised by my colleague, so pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and pursuant to the precedents already existing, we move for the provisional release of our client, Zlatko Aleksovski. This motion is based on the following and, in our view, incontrovertible facts. First, Zlatko Aleksovski was arrested on 8th June 1996 at 8.30 pm by the Croatian police, and on the basis of the request by this Tribunal, and the constitutional provision on the co-operation of the Republic of Croatia with the International Criminal Tribunal of 19th April 1996, and pursuant to these provisions, Zlatko Aleksovski has been in the custody of the International Criminal Tribunal since 28th April 1997. Second, the indictment against Zlatko Aleksovski, in its scope of the charges and its legal foundation, points without our claims to try to compare it to the indictments of the others, is peripheral to the events in Central Bosnia in early 1993. Based on this, the Defence will show that in the case of Zlatko Aleksovski, cumulatively speaking, all four conditions in 65(B) are satisfied and that is (A) exceptional circumstances, the certainty that the accused will appear for trial; (C) that the accused will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person; and (D), the position of the host country. So let me proceed in that very order. (A); the issue is whether the special circumstances do or do not exist. In this context, we will point to several elements. One is the length of the detention. I want to point out that until today, Zlatko Aleksovski has been detained 582 days. I think that this number in itself speaks very vocally, so no additional explanations are needed there. Next I want to point out to the health conditions of Zlatko Aleksovski. Even while in Republic of Croatia, he was treated for various health problems; circulation, problems with blood pressure, spine, et cetera. These are all conditions that do not lend themselves to successful treatment in the conditions of detention. On the other hand, upon his arrival in The Hague, additional health conditions arose, especially psychological ones. They are manifested through insomnia, nervousness, headaches, perspiration, loss of appetite and I should like to just mention to the Trial Chamber the specific fact that he has lost 17 kilograms since his arrival in The Hague, and a loss of concentration. All this can be corroborated by the reports of the prison physician and psychologist. Next the family conditions of the accused. As the Trial Chamber knows, he is the father of two very small children who live with his wife and his incapacitated mother. The entire family in fact lives on the pension of the accused's mother, so the issue is not only the education of the small children but the survival of the whole family. Fourth, we would like to point out the behaviour of Zlatko Aleksovski during the detention. He was the one who asked to work and all tasks that he is given he has been fulfilling conscientiously. He has been very well received in this environment, he is perhaps even favourite there. There have been no incidents relating to him, and if necessary, we request that a formal report be compiled from the detention authorities. So taking into account his behaviour here in the detention unit and the family conditions and everything else, we feel that all these taken together have certain weight, and taken together and interconnected they assume a larger quality so that we can speak of exceptional circumstances from Rule 65(B). The second condition laid out in the same paragraph is the certainty that the accused will appear for trial. I think this condition too has been met, because apart from his personal promise to do so, the promise of the accused and possible surrender of the passport of Croatia, his Croatian passport, we have other arguments to convince the Trial Chamber that there is preparedness of the Republic of Croatia to give guarantees to the Tribunal that they will meet any demand of the Tribunal so that the accused would be present at his trial. These are not empty promises, which is borne out by what has been done so far, which is the fact which I have already mentioned, that is that the Croatian authorities were the ones who arrested Zlatko Aleksovski, to the more recent events, which also speak to the co-operation of the Croatian authorities with the Tribunal, and I refer here to the voluntary surrender of the so-called Vitez group. We also submit that the third condition from Rule 65(B) has been met, which is that the accused will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person. Even the indictment itself, the way it is articulated, it can be seen that Zlatko Aleksovski does not pose such a danger, and if we add to this that in the case of his provisional release, he would reside in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, it is abundantly clear that he would not have a factual possibility to even contact the persons to whom he allegedly would pose danger. Finally, regarding the fourth condition, which is the position of the host country, the Defence submits that this condition has already been met and we point to the letter of the Dutch authorities of 18th July 1996, in the IT-95-14-T, where it states that the government will practically, that is technically, implement the decision -- order of the Tribunal and it is incumbent upon the Tribunal to decide whether there are conditions for provisional release or not. Allow me to sum up. Taking into account the initial provisions, that is the co-operation of the Croatian authorities, the duration of the detention and the marginal role of our client in the charges relating to the events in Central Bosnia in early 1993, the Defence submits, as it has just been presented, that in the specific case of Zlatko Aleksovski, cumulatively speaking, all four conditions from Rule 65(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence have been met. We therefore move that the honourable Trial Chamber, taking into account all facts and circumstances to which we have pointed, as well as the standards of the European Commission for Human Rights based on the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Basic Liberties, in other words the standards that relate to the duration of detention, and I am not going to elaborate on that -- belabour that point, so taking into account all these elements laid out in Rule 65(B), I move that the Trial Chamber decide on the provisional release of our client, Zlatko Aleksovski. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Has the Defence completed its opening statement? If you permit, the issues which you have raised having to do with defects of the form were settled in a decision by the Trial Chamber and then there was another issue having to do with the application for provisional release. As far as that is concerned, the Trial Chamber will consider that and render a decision on that, but I think what you have just made is not an opening statement and that is why I am asking you whether you have anything else to say as an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence counsel would like to reserve the right to an opening statement before beginning its Defence case. The Defence counsel has just availed itself of this opportunity to present these positions which it considers to be of substantive importance and decisive for the further course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not really understand what you said. Could you tell me again what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence wishes to underline that it reserves its right to an opening statement before presenting its own case, that is at the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I do not know whether the Prosecutor has something to say in response to the questions raised by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can assist your Honours by responding to the matters raised in relation to the application for provisional release, we would ask your Honours' indulgence that we may do that at a later stage, because we would like to consider the matters raised in the transcript and do that during the course of this week, if that is permissible. Alternatively, your Honours may consider it not necessary to hear from us in order to make a decision, and in that event, of course, I will leave the matter to your Honours. But if your Honours do seek our assistance, then we crave your indulgence for some time to prepare a response. Your Honours may appreciate that we were taken somewhat by surprise by the application. We do not wish to be critical, but we had not expected it and it is a very serious move and one which we would want to prepare a detailed response to, should your Honours require that assistance. As I say, if your Honours are minded to proceed with the matter in the absence of that, then that is fine by us as well. Your Honours, we are now in a position to call our first witness. I call Charles McLeod. CHARLES McLEOD (sworn)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might like to be seated, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Charles George Alexander McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th March 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you attend your school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a grammar school in Kent in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you left school, where were you first employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in a factory near Stuttgart in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the British army in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that in the month of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was commissioned in September 1983 as a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you serve with the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in what was then west Germany, in Belfast in Northern Ireland, in England, again in Northern Ireland and then back in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your first and then subsequent rank in the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was commissioned as a second lieutenant and I left as a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the army, did you attend university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to King's College London.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We need to go a little slower so the interpreters can get down everything we are saying. Because we are speaking in the same language we are perhaps moving a little too fast. What degree did you obtain at university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have an upper second class honours degree in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then subsequently resign your commission with the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in -- I left the army in June 1992. I actually resigned one year earlier, giving one year's notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then appointed to the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you first based with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was based as a monitor in the regional centre in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you just tell their Honours very briefly the role that was performed by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The ECMM was established as an international monitoring mission by the international community as the conflict broke out in Slovenia, with the aim of facilitating the withdrawal of the JNA from the barracks in Slovenia. As the conflict spread into Croatia and Bosnia, so the mission spread as well into those countries and then around the borders of the former Yugoslavia with the aim of attempting to reduce tension and broker peace, in very simple terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the structure of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ECMM had a headquarters at that time in Zagreb, with regional centres at various points around the country, and co-ordinating centres reporting to the regional centres and monitoring teams reporting to co-ordinating centres, and a monitoring team typically was two monitors, usually of two different nationalities, with a driver and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What role did you play initially with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a monitor working in the regional centre in Zagreb, working on both sides of the contact, the internal contact line within Croatia, between the Serbs and the Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What type of work were you doing, what were you performing, what sort of role were you performing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. In the first instance we were monitoring the withdrawal of troops from the internal contact line and looking to see where heavy weapons, tanks and artillery were being stored, and then again working on both sides of the contact line to attempt low-level humanitarian acts, identifying where people were and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then move to the humanitarian section of ECMM, or was that part of what you have already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having been a monitor working for the regional centre in Zagreb I was then moved to the headquarters, still based in the same building, but as part of the ECMM headquarters based in Zagreb as a member of the humanitarian section within the ECMM headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What role did the humanitarian section perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The humanitarian section was responsible for all aspects of a humanitarian nature which the mission came across, both in terms of humanitarian information or problems which were brought to us and also the reporting of humanitarian information which was seen by our monitors in the field, passing that information on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do in that section, the humanitarian section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was responsible for the tasking of teams to carry out humanitarian activity such as we were able to carry out, fairly limited, the collation of information which was produced by the teams into a report which was then passed on to other people and liaison with largely the international humanitarian agencies working in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you name some of the humanitarian -- international humanitarian agencies with which you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example the ICRC, UNHCR, Deutsche Humanitare Hilfe, the national Red Cross organisation as opposed to the ICRC, World Health Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were ECMM humanitarian activity reports, what are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were reports which we produced on a weekly basis, taking the humanitarian content from the teams' reports which were produced on a daily basis and collating this into a digest of all the humanitarian information which we reported which we then passed on to virtually anybody who asked for it, but primarily the various international agencies. We did this because our monitors went to places and saw things which were on occasions difficult for other people to see, and we felt that it was quite useful for us to be able to use this part of our reporting as freely and as widely as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in the compilation of these reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to an extent I had the idea of doing it and used to sit on a nightly basis and collate the humanitarian bits and type it up and distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you may have touched on this, but what did you see as the main purpose of these reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We felt quite strongly that where we had access to information which either other people did not have or which they would find useful to have corroboration of, that as far as possible we should provide this information to the other agencies who would then be able to react to it. We were not in a position to do very much, but we did have information, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go on mission into Bosnia during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went on a number of missions into northern Bosnia. Initially I was part of a team who were trying to re-establish an ECMM presence in Serb controlled northern Bosnia. As a result of these trips which we had made, we then accompanied a CSC conference on security and co-operation in Europe Rapporteur mission to visit the camps at Manjaca and Trnopolje and having been to those camps, I was then part of teams who accompanied the ICRC when they were releasing detainees from those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go in Christmas 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent Christmas and New Year of 1992 in Kiseljak, which is a town just outside Sarajevo in Central Bosnia. I was there as the ECMM liaison officer at General Morrillon's headquarters, which was the UNPROFOR headquarters in Bosnia. I was there for a period of about four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the ECMM liaison officer, I was responsible for providing our, the ECMM reporting, on a daily basis to Morrillon's staff; I was responsible for being the point of contact between ECMM and UNPROFOR in Bosnia, and as far as possible facilitating the working relationship between those two organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court what happened in the Lasva Valley in April 1993, so far as you are aware as a consequence of your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, there had been a period of relative stability in the area, which had been broken initially in September or October of the previous year, and then again in January of that year, which exploded again in April and led to a conflict between the Croatian people and the Muslim people who had been largely cohabiting in that area and who until that point had been facing a common enemy of the Serbs who were attempting to push south from northern Bosnia into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to the Lasva Valley in 1993, and how is it that you came to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of April/beginning of May 1993, Thomas Osario of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights and, as it happened, Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica, were both at the headquarters of ECMM in Zagreb. They were both discussing the situation which had just occurred with the senior managers of ECMM. They both felt that it would be of benefit if somebody from ECMM could go to the area and could talk to everybody and perhaps report on what had happened so that we had a clear understanding of the events. Both of them felt that they were under-resourced to do this, the regional centre in Zenica was working flat out anyway, and so the decision was taken by the senior managers in the headquarters in Zagreb that I should go down and help undertake an investigation and produce a report -- investigation is the wrong word, but to go, to talk, to speak to people and to produce a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you in fact then went and did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled in on 3rd May and I left on 12th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were there in the Lasva Valley area, who did you work with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working with members of the regional centre based in Zenica and specifically I was working with Jean-Pierre Thebault who was head of the regional centre, and with Eric Friis-Pedersen, who was a Danish monitor based in that regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the purpose of going in was to gather information and so forth. What did you see in more precise terms as the mission that you would perform when you went into the Lasva Valley area at that time in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was setting out to do, what I was briefed to do was to attempt to speak to the military, the political, the humanitarian leaders on both sides of the conflict in order to hear from them what they thought had happened, so we could get an understanding of what they thought had happened and then, if one was going to be ambitious, to perhaps draw some lessons and attempt to try and prevent the same thing from happening again, but without trying to be too ambitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went in on 3rd May, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was based in the ECMM regional headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you go about preparing yourself for this mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zenica, I sat down and read all of the ECMM reports which had been written about the events which had occurred and I got hold of the UNPROFOR reports which had been written about those events, and I produced a list of the dates and the times and the locations so that I built up a picture of what the international community had reported as happening before I tried to speak to anybody, so that I would have as educated an understanding and starting point for those conversations as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did your meetings with officials in the Lasva Valley commence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first meeting was on 7th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke to the mayors of Zenica and Vitez; I spoke to the military commanders in Zenica and Vitez; I spoke to religious leaders in Zenica and Busovaca; I spoke to policemen in Busovaca and I spoke to Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you start out each of these meetings, what did you say when you first introduced yourself to somebody at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started by explaining who I was, that I had come from the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb in an attempt to give slightly more weight to the significance of the conversation we were having, explained that I was here to listen to the point of view, the understanding of the person that I was talking to of what had happened, and -- that is basically it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you use any aids to assist you in these discussions, any material to help the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in most of the discussions that I had I used a photocopied map of the area and I had coloured pens and I would put the map on the table and say to people, "please show me on the map, using the coloured pens, what happened", and in every case this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What position did you take during the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the location of the meeting, but I was either sitting opposite somebody at a table or sitting in their living room, for example, sitting writing notes on my knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I was a little misleading in my question. What position vis-à-vis the arguments or so forth that was taken? Perhaps I should have expressed that better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was basically there to listen and in general I did not question the things which were being told to me, even though on occasion some of the things which were said appeared slightly preposterous, but I felt that given the very limited time that I had, I wanted to hear what people had to say rather than picking a fight with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you indicated a moment ago that you took notes at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you always take notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I took notes on almost every occasion when I sat down with somebody, in order to have a record of the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these notes contemporaneous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the notes so far as you are concerned accurately reflect what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given the limitations of working through an interpreter on all occasions, and the fact that I was not slowing down the pace of the meetings in order to take notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever threaten the person that you were interviewing in order to get them to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the person able to voluntarily give you his or her version of the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the persons that you interviewed appear to understand your questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, because they were giving answers which made sense in the context of the questions I had asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honours? I notice it is 3.30 -- I am sorry, I have got the wrong time. I think it is 4.00. Sorry, your Honour. Were you accompanied during the course of these meetings and if so by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
