utterances.text: I was accompanied and on each occasion it was either Jean-Pierre Thebault or Eric Friis-Pedersen and one of their interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you try and maintain a verbatim record of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as possible on most occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After these meetings, did you then type up the notes that you had taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you still have the hand-written notes of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you believe that you will need to refer to these notes or your typewritten report, entitled "International Ethnic Violence in Vitez", April 1993, to refresh your recollection of some of the details of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be quite useful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you do need to refer to your notes or the report, can you please ask permission of the court before you do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If called upon by the Defence to see your hand-written notes and the court, are you prepared to produce your hand-written notes for that purpose, for their inspection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the Croat forces in Bosnia at the time when you were there in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If at any time you need to look at your report, please tell me so. What was the name of their political organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this political group backed by any other outside organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly appeared to be backed by the HDZ in Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ascertain this from the research and investigations that you carried out while you were in -- not only in Bosnia but in Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the local headquarters or bases of the HVO at that time, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were bases, I imagine brigades based in Novi Travnik, in Vitez, in Busovaca and in -- wherever I was at Christmas 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness have leave to refer to his report, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who were the forces opposing the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially then the Serbs based to the north of them, and then during this conflict it was the ABiH, the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the supreme headquarters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What political organisation backed the army of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what the name of the local army of BiH force was in the area? What corps was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: III Corps, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the III Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may look at my notes, please? He was a gentleman called Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By referring to your notes, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a meeting with him on 7th May in his headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly one of his deputies was called Ramiz Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a meeting with him, again in the headquarters, on 9th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of the III Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to their headquarters in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What other international organisations did you have contact with when you were in the Lasva River valley area in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had meetings with the ICRC and I had meetings with UNPROFOR and specifically that was BritBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And BritBat is an abbreviation for "British Battalion", is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: British battalion based in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the BritBat battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Colonel Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said earlier that your first meeting took place on 7th May 1993. What was the first local official that you met on 7th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the mayor of Zenica, and his name was Besim Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Spahic, what did he tell you about the aims of Belgrade and Zagreb in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His view as he expressed it was that both Belgrade and Zagreb had aspirations to conquer Bosnia, in extremely simple terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say the HVO had done in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that the HVO had attempted to partition and block off parts of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had tried to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that they had attempted to contain the situation and to prevent the area from being blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you spoke to the mayor of Zenica, did he give you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He gave me a number of documents including a list of people whom he said he believed were missing from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the people that he said, or did you come to know the ethnicity of the people that he said were missing from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was talking about Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you happen to know what ethnic group he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that I now show you -- your Honours, a copy of this has been supplied to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, this might be a good point to take a break. We are going to have a break now. We will begin again at 4.00. (3.40 pm) (A short break) (4.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can we continue now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. McLeod, would you please look at the document that is now shown to you, and might a copy be given to the Defence as well, please? Perhaps that might be allocated the next number in order of Prosecution Exhibits, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 5, Prosecution Exhibit 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, do you recognise this document that you are now shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the list of names that I was given by the mayor of Zenica in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the bottom half of the document, there is numbers 1 to 13, and a list of apparently positions typed in English. Was that on the document when you received it or has that subsequently been added to the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see if you look at the piece of paper a line through the middle and what I did was I photocopied the original list on to the subsequent page with the list of translations at the bottom and my handwriting, 1 to 13, is on the left-hand side of the original list, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do with the document when you received it from the mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I kept it with me and I attempted in a small way to find out what had happened to the people on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ultimately, did you use this document as an annex or an appendix to the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as you can see in the top right-hand corner of the document which you have, it was appendix 2 to annex A to the report which I had written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours, I tender that for admission. Did you then, after speaking with the mayor of Zenica, did you then proceed to speak to the mayor of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you happen to know what his ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you about the people that were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that a number of people had been detained and that -- can I refer back to my notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that they had released all the people who had been arrested in Vitez, except for 13 people, because they needed to be asked questions in Busovaca and Kaonik, that was the note that I wrote of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By Kaonik, what did you understand by reference to that at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that stage I did not know what he was referring to. By the time I had finished writing my report, I knew he was referring to the prison at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met with the deputy commander of the III Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ramiz Dugalic, did he say anything to you about the HV operating in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, turning to my notes, he told me that during the cease-fire which had occurred, the HVO had brought in new forces and he said they had also brought in the HV, the Croatian army and he said that in Mostar there were two brigades of HV. That was what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he mention anything to you about the 13 Muslim officials from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and again referring to my notes if I may, he said that 13 members of the SDA and civil government were arrested in central Vitez. He said they were now in Kaonik and he said that the -- he alleged that the plan was that they should be arrested and the fear was that they should be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the date of this meeting with Dugalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 9th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the same day, 9th May 1993, did you have a meeting with the imam of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you have that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him in his house in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you have the meeting with him there? Why did you have the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the meeting with him because I had intended to meet leaders on both sides of the contact line from both communities, and I had already met with two Croat priests working in and near Zenica, and so in order to balance the picture, I wanted to speak to a Muslim religious leader, and I met him in his house because that was where he was when I went to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under whose control was the town of Busovaca at the time that you met the imam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town was controlled by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met the Croat priests in Zenica, under whose control was that town at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was controlled by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was it that you met with the religious leaders? Why did you select them as people to meet with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in my experience and as appeared to be borne out by the facts, they were people who were in touch with the local civilian population in areas where there were otherwise no military or political leaders to whom one could talk, because these were areas controlled by the opposing party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Croat priests in Zenica tell you of oppression that had been inflicted upon Croat people by Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they listed specific events and gave me details of the events which they were aware in some detail, which is recorded in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the imam in Busovaca? Did he relate to you incidents that had occurred to Muslim people in the community in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He described the environment in Busovaca for the Muslim population as being isolated. They had no contact with Zenica, they were confined to their homes, they were not allowed to worship in the mosque. He said that supplies of food were short. It was not a particularly comfortable existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything about Muslim houses or homes in the Busovaca region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and again referring to my notes, he said that in Ocenici, between 20th and 23rd April, five women had been killed, and the houses had all been burnt, and the funerals had just been carried out for these five women, which was why he referred to that incident. He said that in Jelinak the HVO had burnt all the Muslim houses and then the Muslims had burnt the Croat houses, so there was a degree of burning going on on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were there at the house, did anyone else arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I was finishing the conversation and indeed a meal which had been prepared while we were there by his wife, which we were forced to eat, to share, which was an uncomfortable experience, the local Croat police arrived, came into the house and asked us what we were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say it was an uncomfortable experience; because you knew the fact that they were short of food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, having had an explanation of the fact that there was very little food to then be invited to share a meal which was being prepared as we sat there was an uncomfortable experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that the HVO police arrived. When they arrived, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Croatian police, I cannot remember whether they were military police or civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was leaving and I said I would accompany them back to the police station so that we could have a conversation, because they were keen to talk to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went back to the police station, did you discover whether or not they were civilian or military police? Refer to your notes if you need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the police station, I then had a meeting with the chief of the civil police in Busovaca, a representative of the regional police and the deputy chief of the military police in Busovaca, so civil and military together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the chief of the civil police that you met with in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Nikica Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again referring to your notes, during the course of your discussion with the police, did the issue of prisons arise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, initially we had been discussing the case of a girl who had been raped a couple of days before. They were explaining the process which they were carrying out to investigate the case and explaining what would happen to the suspects that they had in the case, and so from that we entered a discussion about prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they tell you about prisons as they operated in the region at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reading from my report, they said that: "Zlatko Aleksovski is responsible for Kaonik prison, it is HVO, not run by the police, it is under the jurisdiction of the military court in Travnik." That was the note that I wrote of the explanation which they gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 10th May 1993, did you then go to Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accompanied Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were travelling with two interpreters, but at the meeting, we were only accompanied by Jean-Pierre Thebault's interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this day, on 10th May 1993, where did you set out from, what town did you set out from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove from Zenica along the road towards Busovaca and then up to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By what means did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were driving in ECMM marked armoured Mercedes four-wheel-drive vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As you got to the camp itself -- perhaps I will withdraw that. Had you ever been to the camp at Kaonik before this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As you got to the camp, did you see any guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniform, to my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not they were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no specific memory of whether they were carrying guns or whether they were not carrying guns. Most people were carrying guns, but I cannot specifically remember at that time whether the people that I saw had them or did not have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any idea of how far the camp was from the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having looked at a map subsequently to work out where we were, it was within two or three kilometres of where I knew the front-line had been. I was not aware at that time of precisely where the front-line was, but it was within two or three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Kaonik prison, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went into the first building which we came to, which was a long building and when we arrived, we were taken into an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you ushered into anybody's office in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether the office was specifically designated for somebody, but it was the office in which we met Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this office located in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we walked into the building, it was on the left-hand side before we got up to the main prison corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the person that you accompanied there, Jean-Pierre Thebault, whether he had been there before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether he had been there before or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were ushered into the office where you met Mr. Aleksovski, who was in that office with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout there was Mr. Aleksovski, myself, Jean-Pierre, Jean-Pierre's interpreter and then from time to time there was also a female secretary who was attempting to produce a list of prisoners from a computer. She came and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The interpreter that you took in with you into the office, were you confident or reasonably confident of her ability to interpret accurately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in light of the experience that I had of working with interpreters, she appeared to be entirely competent and because she was working for Jean-Pierre, I assume that he had taken for himself the best interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Aleksovski, was it a cordial meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the atmosphere during the meeting was relaxed, we had a fluent conversation, it was a cordial meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did most of the talking on the side of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jean-Pierre Thebault did most of the talking and I sat and wrote notes during most of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion, were you writing on a desk or -- were you resting the book on a desk or on your knee? Maybe you cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain. I think I was probably resting on my knee, but there may have been a low table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you earlier if you had a copy of your hand-written notes with you so that you could refer to them. Do you have these hand-written notes of the meeting that you had with Mr. Aleksovski on 10th May 1993, is that with you in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the purposes of your formal report, did you later prepare a typed version of your hand-written notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you prepared this typewritten version, did you rely upon the hand-written version of the notes that you took when you were at the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did and I typed an almost verbatim copy of the hand-written notes. I made a number of small corrections for grammatical mistakes, but leaving most of them as it was, and I added a couple of comments of my own inserted within the text as I had written it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, are there any material differences between the hand-written notes and the typed report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately, if you can remember, how long after you had taken the hand-written report at the meeting of 10th May 1993 did you type up the typewritten version, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been within the next three days. I cannot remember whether I wrote this report immediately afterwards or within the next couple of days, but the report was published on the 15th, so it was within the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Will you look at the document I am about to show you, please, and again might a copy of this be given to the Defence. Might it be given the next number in order of Prosecution Exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at that document that is now shown to you, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the typewritten report of my visit to the prison, which appears in my report as annex O.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the document that we have been referring to in the previous questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Very slowly, because it has to be interpreted, would you please read this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. If I go too fast just shout. So this is annex O to the report dated 15th May 1993. The date of the meeting is 10th May 1993, and this is the, "visit to Kaonik prison, director Zlatko Aleksovski": "Mr. Aleksovski used to work in Zenica prison. He thinks that his prisoners are lucky because he is a professional who knows how to handle them. "The job is difficult regardless of the kind of prisoners. The problem is that they have a large number of people and there is still some fighting in the area. There is quite a lot of fear because of the fighting, people feel threatened and there is fear on both sides, both from those inside and out. "The problem is that someone needs to provide certain guarantees to both prisoners and jailers, because some people are not strong enough and you expect reactions from them under certain conditions. "So far they are not bad problems that they could not solve or that would cause chaos. This can be checked by talking to people. There is no kind of mistreatment. "More or less all the rules of the Geneva Convention are obeyed in most cases. There is some flexibility because he is used to respect the rules of the prison in Zenica. "In January this year, he was here when 400 Muslims were arrested here. During this conflict the situation was worse because fighting was close and there was a bigger conflict and the outcome of the conflict was not certain. If you are familiar with the present situation you can see that there is pressure on the HVO. "ICRC from Zenica visit very regularly, three or four times in the last conflict. In case they happen to have two or three more prisoners arrive, they inform ICRC. I think ICRC have no objections in regard to my work. I cannot guarantee for the others, but certainly for my work. "The biggest problem is that we are poor, there is a lack of food and money. There is a lack of food and we do not think that we have good conditions here. The cells were quickly constructed and not designed for their current purpose. "Currently, there are 79 Muslim prisoners. There were more: on 16th April we had 107 prisoners, on 6th May we had 109 prisoners and on 9th May we also had 109 prisoners." At this point he was referring to a document which he was showing to us. He said: "This is an appeal for the release of five people from ICRC, an appeal for the release of ICRC drivers, arrested on 14th April in Novi Travnik. When we speak of those who work for ICRC and do not, I have sent them a letter saying that I would like to warn them who they engage within their humanitarian organisation. These are soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You can move a little bit faster. I think we are doing well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we have my comment: "When questioned about the charges against the prisoners being held in the prison, there was a complicated answer: "This prison was not established just for this conflict. It is the military prison for the whole region of Central Bosnia. So all these Muslims arrested during this conflict are in the charge of HVO of Busovaca and Vitez. He wants to stress that they (the HVO) do not do their job professionally and officially. "This prison is just to hold them." Then again he was showing us a document: "For example here is the release document signed by local brigade commander authorising the release or exchange of a prisoner. "Another problem is that almost all of the staff were mobilised and taken to the front-line, so one of his guards is 60 years old, and most of them are unable to do their jobs when he is absent. He lives here because his flat was emptied in Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the words "he lives here", who did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksovski was explaining that he lived at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The two basic problems are lack of food and a lack of security staff. The third problem they are trying to solve is the problem with those people who are arrested, who are brought here without any selection. But he must stress that the women and children are not brought here. "Both soldiers and civilians are brought. The explanation that he is given for the civilians is that they are brought for their protection. With the soldiers it is obvious. "The fourth problem is internal exchange. There were a great number of those agreed by local commanders or other important people within the local community. "Or often someone is given permission to be released because they know someone important. Thus we are left with the poor who do not have such good relations with the rich and powerful. The only comfort, if that is what it is, is that the most important people from Vitez were also brought here. "Fifth is the kind of work that the prisoners have to do. Because I know that the Geneva Conventions do not allow prisoners to be taken for any work if their lives are in danger. I have been warned about that by the ICRC as well. "But I am not the only one responsible for this, because I just carry out orders. The brigade commanders in Busovaca and Vitez give them. Not that I want to avoid my responsibility. Because I am not the one who releases people to do the work. In order to clear it up, I went with Beatrice of the ICRC to the commander in Busovaca where she protested for the people to be taken to work under such conditions. "She was given the answer I almost completely agree with. We here actually do not have enough people to do the security jobs. Someone had to dig the trenches and it happened that the men to do that were the prisoners. On the contrary it would happen that Busovaca would be occupied and I do not need to explain what would happen if Mujahedin occupied it, so in a way the Muslims protected Busovaca. "This compared to the Geneva Convention is not right, but regarding the need for the trenches to be dug I think that it is right. One day we were digging trenches and the Muslims attacked our position, and everyone tried to run away. So when we gathered together we found that two men were missing. There had been six of them digging trenches".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Might I interrupt for a moment please? I believe that if we are going to read this entire document -- we are now on the third page only. Could you submit this report as an exhibit and allow the witness to summarise the essential points of the document? I invite the Prosecutor to proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour, I will tender it as an exhibit. I know the process is taking a long time, but the document itself, of course, is central to the Prosecution case, and I was anxious for it to be read into the transcript. I could ask the witness to read it at normal speed, which would mean that it would be completed quickly and it does not matter that the translation may be not so accurate. In that way we could dispose of it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps the document could be read a little more quickly, I believe that actually the interpreters have the opposite problem at the moment, it is a bit too slow. All right? Can we go ahead please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you can pick up from where you are and read it at normal speed. If there is any difficulty with the interpreters, perhaps they may be good enough to indicate they are having difficulties and we can deal with it then. Would you mind reading it at ordinary speed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly: "Not all of the prisoners are military. They do not have details of who is military and who is civilian. It is the problem of the military police and the intelligence organisation. "They have released, or rather will release the civilians. None of the Muslims have been charged with anything, other than being members of the BiH army. "The prison is for the whole of Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. But they can not even get a kilo of bread up from the south, let alone a prisoner. So they have several small prisons in the districts. "They have space for 80 and have about 40 criminals as well as the Muslims. "I do not think anyone would accept responsibility for the small prisons. According to my personal estimation I would consider these small prisons as private prisons, no one would take responsibility. For example the music school in Zenica. "But I would like to stress that in Busovaca there are no double prisons, for example in Zenica there are several places outside the main prison. "As far as I know, my father-in-law was taken a few days ago by a terrorist group: 7 Muslim brigade. My mother-in-law had a phone call that he is alive and well and will be killed if any civilian in Busovaca is killed after 7th May at 11.30. "When they took my father-in-law they gave her a kind of receipt where it is written III Corps BiH and name of those who were there: Delalic Nasid and Perehda Besim were the people who did it. "The brother of one of my guards was taken to the main prison, and since I used to work there I asked about him and was told he was there. But when the brother called he was told he was not there. His name is Janic Ilja Dragan. "I do not know about the cinema in Vitez, but I know they are kept in some basements. I was told that last night, when I talked to prisoners from Vitez. They said that in some basements conditions were good and some were bad. "Concerning the problems within his guards he has four men whose brothers were killed in the front-line and a lot of people from Busovaca lost members of their families. In such critical situations people used to drink too much. You can imagine what happens when such drunk people come to take revenge. "Would you shoot a man who has lost his brother to stop him from abusing a Muslim? In order to restrain them without shooting my guard are not carrying weapons. You will see that those who have contact with the prisoners do not carry weapons. All the weapons here are some old-fashioned rifles and we only carry them at night. "It can be very dangerous because we work here with people, we are responsible for their lives. You should check with them. "I do not want to avoid my responsibility. I do not know the exact date when the cease-fire was agreed, when the UN came to separate the two sides. At that very moment when the UN went to separate them, the BiH killed Muslims because they should know that only Muslims kill Muslims. "Therefore relatively they are all secure here. To confirm that, they should see that you carry flak jackets, outside it is more dangerous. "I want to repeat once again, if we did not have trenches dug then who can say what would have happened? Presently there is not large scale fighting. There are incidents, snipers are active. A civil policeman was killed yesterday. "I have doubts that we will have peace here; I have heard there is a general call-up in Zenica. "In Jelinak we gathered all the women and children into one house to protect them from the men who had lost brothers. Then we told them to go to Zenica. They escorted them on foot to the petrol station, then told them to go to Zenica. "BiH now control Jelinak. The village was burnt at the very beginning, on the second day of fighting. We were on one side and they were on the other. They started shelling and we withdrew from our positions. Then they burnt the houses. All of them have been burnt. "For example our people from Kacuni were all expelled and then they burnt the whole village. The first case happened in Dusina, where BiH entered the village and killed all the Croats. They actually cut the heart out of the body of the commander. This was back in January. "Comment: we then went to look at the prisoners. One man asked if he could ask a question, and then asked why he was being held. Aleksovski said that in this case he knew, having spoken to the men who brought the prisoner in. He had been arrested for his own protection because he was tending a field in a conflict area. "I commented quietly that if it had been me, I would have sent him to Zenica for his protection, rather than putting him into a cell. Aleksovski said that in that case, since the man was clearly a civilian, we could take him back to Zenica with us. He told the man to take his coat and leave the cell. While we were still talking they organised a car to take him back to the point where he was picked up. "This prompted a discussion of whether all the other civilians who were being held for their own protection should be released, which was continued once we had seen looked into the other cells in the building. "We spoke to several men who had been arrested in Vitez on 16th April. They said that they were civilians and asked when they would be released. For the most part they were teachers and engineers. All of them said that they had been arrested at home. The list of Muslim prisoners held is at appendix 1. "In every cell at least one prisoner made a point of making a short statement to the effect that all the prisoners were being well treated and had no complaints about their conditions. These statements were reminiscent of the speeches made to the commandant of Manjaca by prisoners when they were released. "On the question of the definition of a soldier, there was a long discussion centred on the argument that any man between the ages of 16 and 60 was a soldier, so there could be no civilians. But at the same time some of the men held were clearly civilians, so the definition of a soldier as someone who was captured during combat, wearing a uniform with a weapon in his hand was offered as the alternative. Aleksovski finally said that he would get the military police to decide, and would send us lists of the soldiers and civilians as soon as they had. Comment ends. "For the civilians, HVO actually offered unconditional release and I think in a day or two it will be achieved for civilians. For soldiers, things are more complicated, because III Corps require a one-for-one exchange. "I do not know how many other soldiers they have or we have, so there are some problems. I promise that on my part I will do my best for the civilians as a positive sign. Most probably these two first will be released because I cannot provide a 100 per cent guarantee for the others. "Comment: he claimed not to have seen the joint order signed by Petkovic and Halilovic, ordering the release of all civilians, so we said we would fax him a copy. "I will go with you to both HQs and will give them a guarantee that I will act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. He said that he would fax us lists of all those who had been brought into the prison, all those who had left, and all those who remained." That was the end of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that report, your Honours. Mr. McLeod --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence counsel is opposed to the use of this document that has been read as evidence, because it is a combination of a report by Mr. McLeod and quotations of alleged statements by the accused, Zlatko Aleksovski. That statement, under no circumstances, was given under formal conditions that would be required and therefore cannot be considered as evidence in the proceedings. Defence counsel is making this objection in line with the previously expressed position that it will vehemently oppose any attempt to use circumstantial evidence. Therefore in our view, this document, which is a compilation, combining a report with alleged statements by the accused, cannot be admitted into evidence, and we would request that you rule in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, the document in question is not a document which would fall into that category of documents or confessions which the Rules of Procedure and Evidence deal with, which impose upon, for example, members of the Office of the Prosecutor certain conditions requiring for example that counsel be present, that the person be entitled to decline to answer any questions necessary and so forth that are set out in the Rules. Those provisions contained in the Rules of the Tribunal are importantly there because they deal with people who are either determined as suspects or people who have been indicted with charges, and they need to be given the caution that anything they say may be taken down and used in evidence. Your Honours, this is a statement taken contemporaneous with the events. It is a statement taken at the time that the alleged offences, during the period of time that the alleged offences are said to have occurred. It is direct evidence of the events and circumstances of that time. It is precisely the same as if a witness came before you at that time and said that, "in May 1993, I was a prisoner in the Kaonik prison and I saw the following things, or I heard Mr. Aleksovski say the following things". All of that would be clearly and properly admissible. What might happen several years later, when the Office of the Prosecutor proceeds to present an indictment for confirmation, and a person is indicted, a whole of different and separate circumstances then prevail. That has no bearing on what happens here. You have heard evidence from this witness that it was voluntary; you have heard evidence from this witness that he took a contemporaneous note of events and that he wrote down what was said at the time. It is not written down in the way that you would find a record of interview maybe recorded between a professional police investigator and an accused person, certainly not, but it is the very best thing to it, but it does not have to be, your Honours, because it is evidence taken directly from the time that the offences were being committed. In our submission, your Honours, there is no suggestion in any way that this was involuntary. In fact if anything the circumstances speak for themselves. The statement was taken in the prison, in the office of the Mr. Aleksovski. The witness has attested to the fact that he did not place any pressure upon Mr. Aleksovski or on any of the people he interviewed; he did not offer any opinions as to whether he thought what was said was right or wrong. He made it very clear, your Honours, in his evidence that the whole purpose of him being there was to obtain their views of the events, and he used his best endeavours to achieve that end. The fact that the statements were taken contemporaneous with the events, contemporaneous with what was said, and was later produced in this report, make them clearly admissible and there is no prohibition that I know of in any national system that would prevent the admission of this document, and, your Honours, there is certainly nothing under the Rules of the Tribunal which would go to prevent the admission of this document into evidence, and I submit that it properly should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: As regards this question, the Trial Chamber will accept the document, because it is part of the witness's testimony, and as stated in Rule 98, the Trial Chamber can receive any documents which it considers to have probative value. 99, excuse me, not 98. And the Trial Chamber accepts the document. The Rule is 99(C) -- 89(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. 89, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We will now continue with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. Mr. McLeod, just looking at the document that has now been admitted into evidence and in particular at the second paragraph on the first page of the document, do you see there in the last line of the second paragraph the words "threatened and there is fear on both sides, both from inside and out". The words "inside and out" as they appear there, what did you understand was being described at the time when you took down the notes, by reference to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was referring to the captives and the captors, so inside and outside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going down if you would for me please to the fifth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, your Honours. Defence counsel has an objection again, because the witness, as an eyewitness of the events, is saying what he thought the accused thought. Defence counsel argues that it is not possible for the witness to testify about what somebody else thinks. He can testify about what somebody else said or did, but not what somebody else thought. That is the gist of the Defence's objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will take into consideration your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I will be asking a number of questions along this similar line, perhaps I should respond very briefly to what my friend has raised in his objection, in terms of endeavouring to explain my position, if I may. Your Honours, I am not at all asking this witness to tell us what Mr. Aleksovski meant, nor am I asking this witness to try and explain what was in Mr. Aleksovski's mind at the time when he said something. I am asking the witness to tell us what he understands by something that was taken down by him. Your Honours, there is always some ambiguity in language and sometimes it is difficult to know one way or the other what someone means when they write something down. It does not go necessarily to prove that Mr. Aleksovski meant that, but it does assist, in our submission, if this witness is permitted to explain what he understood it to mean when he wrote it down. In many cases during the course of conversation, people say things and if we are taking a literal writing of what was said, people say things but there is greater meaning because of the relationship in the conversation. When it appears in written form, particularly when it is taken down rapidly, sometimes the meaning becomes either ambiguous or sometimes it is lost, so it is only to that extent that I am seeking to do it and I am certainly not asking this witness to tell us what Mr. Aleksovski meant by that statement. Mr. McLeod, in the fifth paragraph on page 1, you have reported that Mr. Aleksovski is saying "more or less, all the rules of the Geneva Conventions are obeyed in most cases". Then he says: "There is some flexibility because he is used to respect the rules of the prison in Zenica." What did you understand by that remark when you wrote it down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that since he had been a professional jailer at the prison in Zenica, he understood how a jail should be run and therefore he was saying that he had some understanding of how the Geneva Convention should be applied to the running of a prison and he was also using his knowledge as a professional jailer to ensure that the prison was run along the lines in which he ran it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first sentence on the fourth page reads: "Would you shoot a man who has lost his brother to stop him from abusing a Muslim?" Again, in the context of the conversation that was going on between you and Mr. Aleksovski, what did you understand that sentence to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was asking whether we felt that it was appropriate, or that it would be appropriate, to shoot somebody in order to protect a prisoner under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the second paragraph on page 5, and this is something where it says: "Reminiscent of speeches in Manjaca." That is something you have said and relates to your own experience, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you mean by that when you wrote that down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said during my introduction, I was present at Manjaca with the ICRC when the ICRC were taking detainees out of Manjaca and I had the very strange experience of watching several hundred men lined up in the snow and then their leaders or nominated members of the Muslim group who had been detained by the Serbs at Manjaca asked permission to make a short speech and then made a short speech thanking the commandant for his care and attention in looking after them while they had been there. As an observer standing there in the snow, this looked like a slightly strained and rehearsed performance being put on for our benefit. That was the incident to which I was referring at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the camp in Manjaca that you had visited in 1992, at the same time as when you visited the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Trnopolje in the Prijedor opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask you to look at this next document that I show you, and also a copy of this has been made available to the Defence -- I would ask that a copy be made available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse us, your Honours. (Pause). Your Honours, it seems we may be short a copy for each one of your Honours, but we will endeavour to correct that as soon as possible. It looks as though we have done it now. Just looking at this document that you are now shown, Mr. McLeod, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of a computer printout which was handed to us at the prison by Mr. Aleksovski, and I understand that this is a list of the prisoners, the Muslim prisoners who he was holding in his prison on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why is it that you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we had been there, he had been at pains to have a list produced for us, he was quite proud of the fact that he had a computer system with computer records on it, and as you could see from the comments made towards the end of my report, in fact he was then embarrassed because the quality of the list was not as accurate as perhaps it should have been and so he then said he would send us subsequent lists, but this was the best he was able to give us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the quality", do you mean the quality of the printing of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The quality of the data as opposed to the quality of the presentation. It was not clear that all of the people on the list were actually all of the people that were present. There were, I think, a number of discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think on the second page of the document at the bottom of the list, although it is not terribly clear on all copies, I am not sure whether it is clear on their Honours' copy, but does the name of the accused appear there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The writing that appears on that document, do you recognise whose writing that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of the manuscript is my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you write on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This writing was done by me as we walked around the prison cells and I was writing comments. Unfortunately I did not think to start writing comments as soon as we started seeing the prisoners, but after a while I switched on and realised I should make a tick or write a comment to be able to refer back to those people I had actually seen. On the first page halfway up on the right-hand side is a telephone number, that is the telephone number which we were given towards the end of our meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Given by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we were given that by Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honours. I think it has been given the next number. I tender it into evidence, your Honour. Now, when you went to see the prisoners, to visit the prisoners after your meeting with Mr. Aleksovski, can you describe the physical structure of the building as best you can remember in terms of where his office was and where the cells were that you went to visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The building itself was a long narrow building. His office was on the front of the building, and it was on the left-hand side as one approached, so if one can imagine a T shape, it was on the foot of the T on the left-hand side. We walked from his office up on to the main corridor which ran the length of the building, and off this corridor were a series of cells on both sides of the corridor with ablutions, from memory I think at the end of the corridor, but I am not certain whether they were at the end of the corridor. We walked in a clockwise direction, so up on to the corridor and turned left and as we came to each cell the door was opened, we went into the cell, we saw the people who were in there, had brief conversations with some of them. Not all of the cells were occupied as far as I remember, so most of the people we saw were on a crescent as we walked around the left, bottom of the top of the left-hand arm and on the right-hand arm of the T, if you can imagine that, was a cell in which there were a couple of Croatian military prisoners also being held there with all of their equipment in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of your tour around the cells, and you spoke of this in your report, you mention a civilian prisoner who Mr. Aleksovski said you could take back to Zenica with you. Did you end up taking that person back to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what actually happened to him. What I saw was that following the interchange that we had, he was told to pick up his things, his coat from the cell, he shook hands with the other members of the cell, left and the implication was that he was then being driven back to the place where he was picked up. In practice, I have no idea what actually happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The prisoners that you saw, did these prisoners appear to be soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the people I saw were dressed in civilian clothes and appeared to be civilians. There were certainly two soldiers that we met, but they were introduced as Croatian military prisoners who had committed some unspecified crime. They were dressed in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also speak in your report of an exchange of prisoners that would take place on a large scale. Do you know whether or not a large-scale exchange of prisoners ever occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain whether a large-scale exchange of prisoners did occur as a result of or immediately following the visit that I had there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you make any suggestions to Dugalic, the deputy commander of the III Corps BiH back in Zenica about releasing Croat prisoners on their part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had a subsequent meeting with Dugalic, I told him what I had seen at Kaonik, I explained to him the problems that we had trying to define who was a civilian and therefore eligible for release and who was not a civilian and I suggested that from his point of view, the one thing which he could do would be to release a number of Croatian prisoners whom he was holding to demonstrate his goodwill and to make it easier then for a number of Muslim prisoners to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So far as you are aware, was this advice followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that they did then release eight or nine Croat prisoners being held by the Muslims and this was observed by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After this meeting you had with Mr. Aleksovski on that one day, 10th May 1993, did you ever see or meet him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. This is the point when the Defence can cross-examine the witness, but I think that it would be better if we did it tomorrow, which will give you a little bit of time to think about the questions that you want to ask. Do you agree to do it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence counsel agrees with your proposal, because we would not like to have to interrupt the cross-examination after a few minutes, so it would be better that we start tomorrow, early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For you Mr. Niemann, there is no problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow at 10.00. (5.20 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
